episodes.title: What is HELUT?
episodes.youtubeTitle: What HELUT Actually Is: Circuits You Can Search, and Where It Loses
episodes.description: A direct answer, not a pitch. Yosys turns Verilog into a netlist of lookup tables and flip-flops; HELUT evaluates that netlist as tensors on Apple silicon. That buys three operations an event-driven simulator does not have: the truth tables become continuous so they can be searched and then re-proved by Yosys and SAT, the same representation runs on encrypted data, and many independent instances ride in one submission. The episode opens on a live run where the carry logic is deleted from a two-bit adder, rediscovered by search, re-synthesized by Yosys, and proven equivalent to behavioural addition over the entire input space, with a corrupted value collapsing the proof. Then it states the losses without cushioning. On matched end-to-end work HELUT measured 8.544 ms against 7.422 ms for 16-worker Verilator at B=65,536: 15.1 percent slower, with no paired crossover through that width, and roughly four orders of magnitude behind at a single instance. On simplification it ties rather than wins: the discovered and hand-designed circuits map identically under one abc -lut 6 recipe, 0 wins, 18 ties, 0 losses. The encrypted path costs hundreds of milliseconds per gate and native-dimension processor checks still fail. No discrete-GPU comparison exists, so no cross-architecture claim is made; unified memory is presented as why host-orchestrated GPU search is practical on hardware you can buy, not as a measured win. What is proven: 65,536 distinct lanes with 589,824 output bits checked and zero mismatches, and one flip-flop repair proven by induction. Epoch C69. Site: https://helut.digitaldefiance.org · Source: https://github.com/Digital-Defiance/HELUT

scenes.voiceover: Watch this. That's a two-bit adder, written as four lookup tables. The first two compute the low sum and the low carry. I deleted the other two. Not disconnected, deleted. Their truth tables are all zeros, so the carry logic is simply gone. Now one command. Real test, running live, under two seconds. The broken circuit misses 14 of 48 output bits. Then the search rediscovers the missing tables. Then Yosys, which had no part in that search, re-synthesizes the result and confirms it computes exact two-bit addition on all 16 inputs. Then a SAT solver proves it across the entire input space. Not sampled. Every case. Last screen, I corrupt one rediscovered value on purpose. The proof collapses and hands back a counterexample. A check that cannot fail is not a check. Verilator is faster than this at simulating circuits. It cannot do that.
scenes.label: LIVE RUN · recorded 2026-09-05 · not a replay

scenes.voiceover: HELUT stands for Homomorphic Edge Look-Up Tensors, and the name is the least useful thing about it. Here is the idea. A lookup table stores the output for every possible input, and those entries are normally exact zeros and ones. HELUT lets them melt into fractions, searches for values that hit a target, freezes them back to binary, and then hands the result to something that had no stake in the answer. Yosys turns your Verilog into lookup tables and flip-flops. HELUT picks up from there and treats that circuit as something you can search.
scenes.headline: What is HELUT?
scenes.subhead: Circuits you can search, not just run.

scenes.voiceover: These are not questions from one forum or one commenter. Engineers, viewers, and Redditors who work with hardware descriptions keep asking the same four, and they are the right questions. Simulators already reproduce Verilog accurately, so what does turning a circuit into tensors solve? Is it faster than compiling that description to native code? If it is not, why should anyone care which chip it runs on? And how does the simplification compare with the logic optimization that already exists? Episode zero is the general answer for everyone, including the two places where the answer is that we lose.
scenes.headline: The questions everyone keeps asking
scenes.subhead: Why tensors · faster than native · why this chip · versus ABC

scenes.voiceover: So what is it, without adjectives. Yosys turns Verilog into a netlist of lookup tables and flip-flops. HELUT takes that netlist and evaluates it as tensors. That buys three operations an event-driven simulator has no notion of. One: the tables become continuous, so you can search them. Erase a function, rediscover it, freeze it back, and let Yosys and a SAT solver check the result. Two: the same representation runs on encrypted data, so one netlist serves both cleartext and homomorphic evaluation. Three: many independent instances ride in a single submission, and every one of them gets checked. What it is not, equally plainly: there is no four-state logic, no X or Z, no timing model, and no behavioural Verilog front end. If you want bit-accurate simulation, use Verilator. It is better at that and it always will be.
scenes.headline: A netlist you can search
scenes.subhead: Three operations a simulator does not have

scenes.voiceover: Same circuit and stimulus; matching digests or the timings are void. This footage preserves the dated asymmetric scope: HELUT's warmed graph against one scalar Verilator loop. Native wins dramatically at one lane; this take first shows a graph-only HELUT win at 65,536. That is amortization, not end-to-end throughput. The final paired receipt keeps preparation, execution, strict readback, and the ordered digest inside both timers, with Verilator on 16 workers. At 65,536 HELUT remains 15.1 percent slower, with no paired crossover. Episode 14 shows the sealed current verdict.
scenes.label: DATED LIVE TAKE · warmed graph vs scalar Verilator · digests matched

scenes.voiceover: Where it does well, and these are the rows I will defend. Batched correctness that is actually checked: 65,536 distinct assignments, all 589,824 output bits compared against their own clear oracles, zero mismatches, and a negative control where corrupting one lane moves the digest and reports the mismatch. Second, cost shape. The warmed graph is close to flat across a 65,536-fold range of work, because it is dominated by fixed submission overhead, while a scalar loop climbs linearly. Read that as amortization, not throughput, and I will show you why on the next screen. Third, the operation nothing else offers: erase a function, rediscover it by search, and have an independent prover confirm it over the whole input space. That now includes one flip-flop, proven by induction.
scenes.headline: Where it does well
scenes.subhead: Checked batching · flat graph cost · search with independent proof

scenes.voiceover: Now the losses. If you only remember one screen from this episode, make it this one. On matched end-to-end work, counting preparation, execution, readback and the same ordered digest on both sides, HELUT measured 8.544 milliseconds against 7.422 for 16-worker Verilator at 65,536 lanes. That is 15.1 percent slower, with no crossover at any width I have tested. At a single instance it loses by roughly four orders of magnitude. On simplification it does not win either: run the discovered circuit and the hand-designed one through the same ABC recipe and they tie, zero wins, 18 ties, zero losses. The encrypted path costs hundreds of milliseconds per gate at production parameters, and the native-dimension processor check still fails. And I have never benchmarked against a discrete graphics card, so I cannot tell you this chip beats that one.
scenes.headline: Where it loses
scenes.subhead: Paired throughput · single instance · simplification · encrypted cost

scenes.voiceover: People hear this next part as brand loyalty, so here is the mechanism instead. This workload is a loop. The host builds candidates, the GPU evaluates them wide, the host inspects the results and breeds the next round, and that repeats thousands of times. On a discrete card every one of those boundaries is a staged copy across a bus, and the accelerator is capped at its own memory. Here the host code, the hand-written Metal shaders, and Metal Performance Shaders Graph all allocate from one physical pool, and the GPU can draw on machine memory. That is why large candidate tensors are practical at all. Capacity is usable, though not free: at degree 1024 with a thousand lanes, resident memory peaked near 6 gigabytes and the tick rate fell to 13.6 per second from about 69. So this is an argument about what is possible on hardware you can buy, not a measurement that the architecture wins. I have never run that comparison.
scenes.headline: Why unified memory is load-bearing
scenes.subhead: host builds → GPU evaluates wide → host inspects → repeat

scenes.voiceover: Here is the part I find most useful, and it is a failure. When I erased an entire small circuit instead of part of one, the search came back fully binary. Every value snapped cleanly to zero or one. But target fitness was -16, so the objective already said the answer was wrong. The independent prover then refuted it over the full input domain, turning that warning into an external check. So zero fractional entries means discrete, not correct. More search did fix this same fixture, 500 generations instead of 120. That makes it a budget-sensitive failure rather than a hard wall, and it is exactly why binarity, fitness, and independent proof must stay separate.
scenes.headline: A clean-looking answer that was wrong
scenes.subhead: Fully binary · target fitness -16 · independently refuted

scenes.voiceover: What is not settled, and two things that just stopped being open. Everything in that cold open was combinational, but the proof loop is not limited to it any more: a state transition behind a flip-flop has now been erased, rediscovered, and proven by induction, with a reset-to-divergence trace when you corrupt it. One flip-flop, not a processor, so read it narrowly. The batch benchmark used to feed every lane the same data, which made its scaling table a memory-traffic measurement rather than throughput. That one is closed too: the shipped path carries 65,536 distinct inputs and checks all 589,824 output bits against per-lane oracles, with 0 mismatches. In a separate 256-lane negative control, corrupting lane 37 moves the digest and surfaces five mismatches. Still closed as a null: put the searched circuit and the hand-designed one through the same ABC recipe and they tie, 18 runs out of 18, so there is no area win to claim. And the encrypted path is still slow and still small, hundreds of milliseconds for a single gate at production parameters. Each has a specific experiment attached. That is the difference between an open question and a hand-wave.
scenes.headline: What is not settled
bullets: Sequential repair now proven: 1 flip-flop, by induction
Batch lanes now distinct: 589,824 bits checked, 0 mismatches
Discovered circuits: same LUT count as hand-designed, 6 vs 6
Encrypted path: hundreds of milliseconds per gate

scenes.voiceover: So why keep going, given all that. Because the bridge is proven and the operations are real, while none of them has beaten an incumbent yet. Both halves of that sentence matter, and it is a research position rather than a product. Where I think it can still win. Encrypted evaluation, because sharing one representation between cleartext and ciphertext is a structural advantage rather than a constant factor. And repair rather than minimization: ABC minimizes a function you already have, while search can recover one you have lost. Those are different jobs, and only the second is open ground. There is also one number that keeps me at it. Across the eight widths I tested, the paired gap narrows every single time: 77 times native at one lane, 3.9 at 1,024, 1.63 at 16,384, 1.35 at 32,768, and 1.151 at 65,536. Eight steps, no reversal. I ran out of fixture before I ran out of trend, because 65,536 is every input a 16-bit adder has. Whether that continues is a prediction, not a result. Where I may well be wrong. Cleartext throughput may never cross, because the digest both sides must compute is already 78 percent of my time. Simplification may stay a null. And the encrypted processor may stay out of reach at native dimensions. Naming them now costs me nothing. Discovering them in public later would cost a lot.
scenes.headline: A research position, stated as one
scenes.subhead: Where it may still win · where I may be wrong

scenes.voiceover: Which is why every claim in this series carries a date. The ledger changes as evidence arrives. Results get measured again and some get withdrawn. One encrypted failure turned out to be a nondeterminism bug rather than a limit, and seven timing rows had understated the code by half. HELUT did not invent torus fully homomorphic encryption, and it has not broken the P1030680 message. The E256 offshoot is not fit for real secrets. I would rather show you the boundary than sell you the middle.
scenes.headline: Corrected in public
scenes.subhead: Re-measured · withdrawn · replaced

episodes.title: The compiler substrate
episodes.youtubeTitle: How HELUT Compiles Yosys Circuits into One Metal Graph
episodes.description: How HELUT parses supported Yosys LUT and flip-flop cells, lowers dependency waves into a Metal Performance Shaders Graph, and uses a batch dimension for independent circuit evaluation and later application experiments. A live three-tier Enigma control recovers one injected lane exclusively, checks the clear netlist against an independent oracle, reproduces the FHPQX historical prefix and crib, and isolates SDV among 200 hypotheses. That receipt is one named validation fixture, not arbitrary-Verilog correctness and not FHE. Epoch C69. Cleartext fitness is not encrypted throughput.

scenes.voiceover: Before the diagram, grade one named path. Tier 1 recovers only injected lane 42, then checks HELUT's clear netlist against an independent Enigma oracle. Tier 2 reproduces the FHPQX historical prefix and finds SIEGFR. Tier 3 ranks SDV above 199 decoys. All three go green, live. This is a strong compiler control because each stage can fail for a different reason. It is not a proof of arbitrary Verilog, and nothing on this screen is FHE.
scenes.label: LIVE RUN · recorded 2026-09-06 · one bounded Enigma fixture · not FHE

scenes.voiceover: HELUT begins with a supported Yosys circuit. It turns each look-up table and flip-flop into tensor operations, then builds one Metal Performance Shaders Graph. A batch dimension lets that graph evaluate many independent circuit states in parallel.
scenes.headline: The compiler substrate
scenes.subhead: Yosys JSON → supported cells → one reusable Metal graph

scenes.voiceover: A Yosys JSON netlist names wires, look-up-table truth tables, and flip-flops. HELUT parses the supported cells and groups independent look-up tables by dependency. It lowers each group into tensor operations and builds one reusable graph. A host loop supplies inputs, advances the clock, and carries state into the next tick.
scenes.headline: A circuit becomes a graph
scenes.subhead: Dependencies determine waves; the host advances sequential state.

scenes.voiceover: A look-up table stores a small truth table. HELUT expands that table into a multilinear tensor operation. A D flip-flop preserves one state bit between ticks; enable and synchronous-reset behavior remain explicit. Alternating state buffers keep combinational evaluation separate from the clock edge.
scenes.headline: Truth tables and state
bullets: Each LUT → multilinear truth-table expansion
D flip-flops preserve state across ticks
Enable, reset, and clock behavior stay explicit

scenes.voiceover: B is the batch dimension. Each row carries an independent circuit state through the same compiled graph. That batching is application-agnostic. I later used it to test and score many historical Enigma hypotheses at once. The blind-control campaign averaged 37.4 million settings per second. Hold on to that number: it is a cleartext rate, and an encrypted tick costs roughly a hundred seconds. Those two figures must never be mixed.
scenes.headline: Many machines, one graph run
scenes.subhead: Independent rows share the schedule without sharing state.

scenes.voiceover: The supported-cell path has run PicoRV32 processor cores, regular-expression and decision-tree demos, a radio receiver matching bytes off the air, and a historical M4 search application. E256 is a later experimental offshoot, not another compiler capability. These examples test compiler breadth; they do not share one security level. The encrypted processor work is real but narrow: a ten-tick boot and an instruction fetch, at reduced wire dimension. That is a functional check, not Linux and not a production encrypted CPU.
scenes.headline: What the supported-cell path has run
bullets: PicoRV32 processor stress tests
Regular-expression and decision-tree demos
Historical M4 application and later E256 offshoot

scenes.voiceover: Next, we keep the circuit schedule but replace clear Boolean wires with encrypted lattice samples. We will define each sample type before showing how blind rotation evaluates a look-up table.
scenes.headline: Next: torus FHE
scenes.subhead: Keep the schedule. Replace Boolean wires with encrypted samples.

episodes.title: Torus FHE
episodes.youtubeTitle: HELUT Torus FHE: From Encrypted Wires to Blind Rotation
episodes.description: A term-first tour of HELUT's torus fully homomorphic encryption path: encrypted sample types, blind rotation, negacyclic kernels, the SING correctness gate (Stimuli In, Golden out), wavefront scheduling, configuration-specific receipts, and open limits. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: One HELUT research path explores torus fully homomorphic encryption, or FHE. In FHE, a circuit can operate on ciphertexts without first revealing the underlying bits. The torus here means values sit on a wrapped number circle, so arithmetic runs around the circle instead of overflowing. HELUT keeps the supported Yosys schedule, but replaces clear Boolean wires with encrypted samples built on lattices: hard problems over regular grids of points.
scenes.headline: Torus FHE
scenes.subhead: Operate on encrypted circuit wires without first revealing their bits.

scenes.voiceover: A learning-with-errors sample, shortened to LWE, carries one encrypted scalar wire. A polynomial form called GLWE supplies the rotating accumulator. A GGSW bootstrap key lets the circuit choose a rotation without exposing the control bit. These are different data structures, not three security grades. The errors in that first name are the point: every sample carries deliberate random noise, and that noise is what hides the value. Each operation makes the noise grow, which is why this episode keeps measuring it.
scenes.headline: Wire · accumulator · bootstrap key
scenes.subhead: LWE carries a scalar wire; GLWE carries a polynomial; GGSW controls rotation.

scenes.voiceover: Blind rotation turns an encrypted input into a look-up-table result without decrypting the wire. In the public path, modulus switching prepares that result for the next stage. HELUT also has a secret-key refresh mode for experiments. That mode is not an end-to-end public FHE path. The scheduler runs independent look-up tables together, while the host advances sequential state.
scenes.headline: Blind rotation selects the answer
scenes.subhead: The public path continues without a secret-key refresh.

scenes.voiceover: The heavy kernel is a negacyclic matrix-vector product. Coefficients that run off the end of the polynomial wrap back to the front with their sign flipped. At degree 1024, native unsigned 32-bit wraparound supplies the modular arithmetic for free.
scenes.headline: Wrap around with a sign change
scenes.subhead: A negacyclic matrix-vector product supplies the blind-rotation muscle.

scenes.voiceover: SING is the correctness gate everything else depends on, and the name spells out the method: Stimuli In, Golden out. In hardware verification, a golden model is the trusted reference implementation. Here that reference is the cleartext netlist simulator. So one set of input vectors runs twice. Through the clear circuit, they produce golden bits. Encrypted, evaluated under blind rotation, then decrypted, they must reproduce those same bits exactly. It is the encrypted equivalent of a scan chain. Three published configurations already clear this gate: the adder, the regular-expression matcher, and the processor at reduced wire dimension. And the rule that follows is deliberately harsh: if SING fails, timing is not discussed at all. A fast wrong answer is not a result.
scenes.headline: Stimuli In, Golden out
scenes.subhead: The golden model is the cleartext netlist.

scenes.voiceover: Look-up tables with no dependency between them can blind-rotate in the same scheduler wave. In one logged configuration, eight SING rows took 10.6 seconds at degree 1024. That number measures the scheduler and the kernels together. It is not the cleartext campaign's settings-per-second rate.
scenes.headline: Independent LUTs share a wave
scenes.subhead: Scheduling and kernels are measured together; campaign throughput is separate.

scenes.voiceover: This is the ledger from re-running the rows after the determinism fix, and the useful thing about it is that it fails in public. The first block is noise measurement only. Those rows never touch the fixed tick path, so they are completeness, not the gate. The second block does exercise it. Five encrypted SING rows pass, including wire dimension 512. The last row does not. C56 at test-poly stride seven exits 133, and the ledger prints FAIL next to it rather than dropping it. 15 pass, one fail. Then the file argues with itself in the footer: a nonzero exit is not automatically a broken claim, because some rows are graded negatives. That sentence is the difference between a results table and a receipt.
scenes.label: PRESERVED RECEIPT · post-fix re-validation · prints its own FAIL

scenes.voiceover: Each published configuration needs three separate answers. Did encrypted output match clear output? Did measured noise stay inside the stated bound? What hardness estimate applies to these exact dimensions? The bar for that noise bound is an error probability of two to the minus sixty-four. One logged configuration clears it with room to spare. A neighbouring one shows why the measurement itself matters: at stride seven it falls short, and stride fourteen does not rescue it by itself either. At 32 samples that same configuration reports minus 48 and does not clear; it only clears once the sample count rises, reaching minus 93.8 at 192 samples. So the bound is sample-starved before it is wrong, and neither result becomes a universal guarantee.
scenes.headline: Three questions, three receipts
bullets: Correctness: did encrypted output match clear output?
Noise: did the measured bound clear its stated bar?
Hardness: which exact dimensions were estimated?

scenes.voiceover: Limits remain. Campaign fitness is cleartext, not FHE throughput. The adder ladder now passes at wire dimensions 256 and 512, because a determinism defect was found and fixed; the earlier failure at 512 was withdrawn, not explained away. Separate checks at full native dimension still fail. The hardness comparison only agrees on some parameter sets, so no single bit-count describes the system. HELUT has not established side-channel or quantum resistance.
scenes.headline: Open limits stay visible
bullets: Campaign fitness is cleartext, not FHE throughput
Native-dimension processor checks still fail
No side-channel or quantum-resistance claim

scenes.voiceover: Next, the circuit returns to cleartext, but its look-up-table contents become variables. TensorLUT relaxes those truth tables to continuous values, searches them on Metal, and checks whether a binary circuit can be emitted.
scenes.headline: Next: TensorLUT
scenes.subhead: Keep the circuit clear, but make its truth tables searchable.

episodes.title: TensorLUT
episodes.youtubeTitle: HELUT TensorLUT: Searching and Emitting Truth Tables
episodes.description: TensorLUT turns supported Yosys LUT truth tables into continuous search variables, evaluates them on Metal, and emits discrete Verilog only when bounded checks pass. A live proof ladder shows six implementation-level certificate checks; 2, 4, and 6 melted LUTs of an 8-LUT adder proving at one budget; all 8 returning a binary but wrong result at that budget; and the same 8-of-8 fixture proving with a larger budget. Analytic completeness remains narrow, while bounded SAT-backed fixtures now extend beyond two tables. This is not arbitrary-topology completeness and not a P1030680 decrypt. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: Read this as two ladders. First, the formal certificate: six implementation-level checks for the objective, emitter, involution structure, and freeze mask. That is not a convergence theorem. Second, a fixed 4-bit adder. Erase 2 of its 8 tables and the searched circuit proves. Erase 4, it proves. Erase 6, it proves. Erase all 8 at the same 120-generation budget and it returns fully binary but wrong: REFUTED, fitness -16. Third screen, same full erase with 500 generations: PROVED. So the old sentence that evidence stops at two tables is no longer true. The analytic theorem stays narrow; end-to-end SAT-backed fixtures now extend beyond two. Arbitrary topology and guaranteed convergence remain open.
scenes.label: LIVE RUN · recorded 2026-09-06 · certificate plus bounded search fixtures

scenes.voiceover: Another HELUT research path is TensorLUT. A look-up table normally has a fixed truth table, stored in a value called INIT. TensorLUT treats those entries as search variables, relaxes them to continuous values, and optimizes the circuit on Metal.
scenes.headline: TensorLUT
scenes.subhead: Search the truth tables, then demand discrete hardware.

scenes.voiceover: The cycle has four stages: melt, score, freeze, and snap. Melting means taking the 64 truth-table entries of a six-input look-up table and letting them hold fractional values, blending between entries instead of choosing. Scoring compares circuit output against target behavior. Freezing holds the parts that must not move. Snapping raises a penalty that pushes every entry back to zero or one, and only then does the emitter write a discrete Verilog circuit.
scenes.headline: Continuous search, binary destination
scenes.subhead: A six-input LUT has 64 truth-table entries.

scenes.voiceover: To test this search on a real stateful circuit, I used an unmodified historical Enigma M4 netlist as one benchmark. It first serves as a zero-error baseline. Attempts to melt every entry, or only the plugboard cone, shattered: thousands of values refused to settle to zero or one. The current bounded experiment freezes the known circuit and searches only an involutive plugboard, meaning one that undoes itself, of at most ten swapped pairs. A blind three-pair recovery passed on a short crib.
scenes.headline: What worked—and what did not
bullets: Unmodified M4 netlist: zero-error baseline
Full-INIT and plugboard-cone melts: unstable
Frozen core + ≤10-pair involution: bounded success

scenes.voiceover: The analytic result is bounded, and the boundary is precise. For one fully observed look-up table, there is a proof that it returns to its target truth table from anywhere inside the snap basin: the region where every entry is already nearer its goal than its opposite. A second certificate extends that analytic bridge to a two-table cascade and emits Verilog. That analytic completeness ladder still stops there. End-to-end evidence now goes farther: fixed ripple adders with 2, 4, and 6 of 8 tables melted prove; all 8 fail at the smaller budget and prove at 500 generations; and a 2-of-16 repair trained on 64 rows proves over all 65,536 inputs. Those are bounded deterministic fixtures, not arbitrary netlists or a convergence theorem.
scenes.headline: Continuous does not automatically mean discrete
scenes.subhead: The analytic result is narrow; SAT-backed fixtures now extend beyond two LUTs.

scenes.voiceover: That M4 benchmark does not turn TensorLUT into an Enigma project, and it is not evidence that P1030680 is broken. TensorLUT supplies no guessed plaintext, key, or decrypt. Searching a look-up-table genotype, searching historical M4 settings in a chosen application, and proposing a new E256 profile in a later offshoot are related experiments, but they are not the same process. None should mutate a live cipher without review.
scenes.headline: Related experiments are not interchangeable

episodes.title: The P1030680 Bombe
episodes.youtubeTitle: The P1030680 Bombe: What We Built, Tested, and Still Do Not Know
episodes.description: Why an Enigma message appears in a HELUT series, and what this chosen application built: historical Bombe context, the blind P1030684 control, Welchman diagonal board, Mulein Board, 628-Future bank, and completed Phase 51.16 bounded stripe. A live known-control grade shows injected substitutions recovered at matching tolerance with 0 of 192 host/Metal mismatches, then shows a synthetic four-letter deletion whose correct splice recovers 25 of 25 deductions while explicitly reporting that board specificity is unmeasured. These are mechanism controls, not target evidence. The campaign uses HELUT's cleartext compiler and batch engine; it produced zero BREAK gates, no key, plaintext, or decrypt. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: Before touching the target, grade the machine on published-key P1030684. Top table: inject zero, 1, then 2 wrong letters. The exact board loses the damaged cases; matching tolerance keeps the true lane. Host and Metal agree, every row reads 0 of 192 mismatches, and this control retains one survivor at each tolerance. Second screen: remove a synthetic four-letter group. The ordinary menu becomes illegal; the correct spliced geometry recovers all 25 forced deductions. Now the line that protects the claim: all 28 wrong splices died under Enigma's self-encipherment rule before reaching the board, so board specificity is unmeasured here. That is a finding, not an embarrassment. These screens grade mechanisms and expose a gap. They contain no P1030680 data, and they do not establish target corruption.
scenes.label: LIVE RUN · recorded 2026-09-06 · published-key control · no P1030680 data

scenes.voiceover: Why is an Enigma message in a HELUT series? I chose it as a concrete, demanding way to exercise the cleartext compiler and batch engine. The target, P1030680, is a 72-letter Enigma M4 message from the M-Thetis network, sent in May 1945. Its printed starting-position table is missing. HELUT tests explicit plaintext guesses, correction patterns, and rotor settings against that message. This episode separates a local stop, a physically valid candidate, and an actual break.
scenes.headline: The P1030680 Bombe
scenes.subhead: Why this problem · what we built · why the message remains unbroken

scenes.voiceover: Operational Enigma was not mathematically unbreakable without a crib. Polish cryptanalysts built the foundational attack, and British work by Alan Turing, Gordon Welchman, operators, and engineers extended it. A crib is a plausible plaintext fragment aligned with the ciphertext. Cribs supplied powerful constraints alongside procedures, traffic analysis, captured material, and machine weaknesses. Here the narrower question is what those methods can establish for one short message with no verified crib.
scenes.headline: Enigma was breakable. This message is still unbroken.
scenes.subhead: Cribs were powerful constraints, not the whole history of the break.

scenes.voiceover: The archive leaves little leverage. There are 72 letters and no depth: no second message encrypted at the same setting. No broken M-Thetis corpus supplies a verified crib, and the printed table of starting positions, called the Grund table, is missing. The naval indicators narrow the search by less than one bit. Three other-network day keys score like noise. A sister message shows transcription errors are possible, but does not prove this target is corrupted.
scenes.headline: The target starts with missing information
bullets: 72 letters · no depth · no verified M-Thetis crib
Lost Grund table · indicators contribute <1 bit
Possible transcription error, not established corruption

scenes.voiceover: Before drawing conclusions about the target, HELUT ran the same path without revealing the answer on known message P1030684. Across 15.96 billion settings, two stops survived. The correct rotor configuration, all ten plug pairs, and readable German were recovered. The archived rerun took 427 seconds, averaging 37.4 million settings per second. This validates the tested path when the crib is true. It does not validate any target crib.
scenes.headline: First prove the path on a blind control
scenes.subhead: P1030684 recovered the rotor configuration, all ten plugs, and German plaintext.

scenes.voiceover: A Bombe turns one crib alignment into a graph called a menu. Each edge represents the Enigma scrambler at one message step. The diagonal board starts from one proposed plug pair and propagates the constraints. A disconnected menu can satisfy one component while leaving another untested, creating a ghost stop. HELUT therefore asks whether all components fit one plugboard made of at most ten disjoint pairs. The known control passes. The recurring target stops tested here do not. Even a physical completion is only a candidate.
scenes.headline: A stop is not a break
scenes.subhead: Disconnected constraints can create ghost stops.

scenes.voiceover: One wrong crib letter can make exact propagation reject the true key. The Mulein Board first runs the exact graph, then retries the smallest recorded sets of deleted edges. It preserves the ten-pair limit, keeps the seed connected, and records every dropped edge. In the known control, one to three injected errors defeated the exact board. Matching tolerance recovered the true setting with all 25 forced plug deductions correct. The host and Metal research path test up to three deletions; the production bank reports exact or one-edge cases only. This is a sensitivity control, not evidence that P1030680 is corrupted.
scenes.headline: Delete before closure—and record the repair
scenes.subhead: Exact first. Minimal edge deletions next. Provenance always preserved.

scenes.voiceover: A Future is one fully specified crib and correction geometry. The current manifest contains 628: 314 unchanged alignments and 314 hypotheses with a four-letter gap. One shared 80-step-by-26-letter Enigma trail feeds four parallel lanes. On the known control, the fresh end-to-end suite agrees across source RTL, post-Yosys RTL, clear JSON, and TensorLUT, then catches wrong delta, setting, and seed controls plus bounded combined indel-and-garble repairs. The host deduplicates and verifies each compact target receipt. That is not final replay: 41 exact post-gap hits still await geometry-aware full-message replay, and 4,103 one-edge repairs await correction replay before any break gate. This is a cleartext mechanism grade, not FHE and not P1030680 evidence.
scenes.headline: 628 Futures share one M4 trail
scenes.subhead: Each Future is one fully specified crib and correction geometry.

scenes.voiceover: The setting-zero preflight checked all 628 Futures and retained 15 one-edge repair candidates. It opened no break gate. Production then covered settings one through 255 on the same fixed shell. It checked 4,163,640 receipts and retained 4,184 host-verified candidates; that count excludes the 15 preflight repairs. Forty exact identity hits failed plugboard completion. Forty-one exact post-gap hits await full-message replay. Another 4,103 one-edge repairs await correction replay. No candidate reached a break gate. The run produced no scored plaintext, key, or decrypt.
scenes.headline: What Phase 51.16 actually covered
bullets: Setting 0 preflight: 15 repairs · 0 gates
Settings 1–255 production: 4,184 candidates · 0 gates
One fixed shell; settings 256–456,975 and other shells remain open

scenes.voiceover: For this shell, settings 256 through 456,975 remain open, as do all other shells. More than 82 percent of candidates in the leading four-letter-gap family paired with translated identity states. That does not eliminate a real gap at another boundary. It does make another same-shaped stripe low-information. Next, replay the 41 exact post-gap hits with their full geometry, then deduplicate and explicitly test the strongest identity repairs.
scenes.headline: Replay before widening
scenes.subhead: Most settings, every other shell, and legacy coverage gaps remain open.

scenes.voiceover: This campaign is one application of HELUT, not the definition of the project. The tested machine recovered the known control. For the target, it covered one shell, all 628 hypotheses, and only settings zero through 255. No break gate opened, and P1030680 remains unbroken. Next, I follow a separate idea that grew from the attack lessons: E256, an experimental rotor-inspired offshoot.
scenes.headline: A machine, a bounded result, and an open message
scenes.subhead: One HELUT application ends with public receipts—not a decrypt.

episodes.title: E256 — Turning Enigma Inside Out
episodes.youtubeTitle: E256 Architecture: Turning Enigma's Weaknesses into a Design Brief
episodes.description: How one HELUT application led to E256, a separate experimental crypto offshoot; what its anti-fascist counter-history means to its author; and how the byte-wide reciprocal machine is built. Covers base 256, the attack-response matrix, ten-access byte path, state schedule, and host/RTL boundary. Experimental; not for real secrets. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: E256 is not a third HELUT pillar. It is a separate experimental crypto offshoot inspired by the Enigma application. After using HELUT to study historical M4 search, I turned selected attack lessons into a new design brief. E256 is a byte-wide stream construction inspired by rotor machines. It is not a repaired M4, and it is not compatible with historical Enigma.
scenes.headline: E256
scenes.subhead: A byte-wide reciprocal machine inspired by rotor structure—not a repaired M4.

scenes.voiceover: Foundational Polish cryptanalysis, then work by Turing, Welchman, operators, engineers, and captured intelligence made historical breaks possible. As a trans engineer, I also read Turing's persecution as a warning about state power against queer people. Reversing the symbolism matters to me: study a fascist war machine, publish its weaknesses, and build defensive tools against modern neo-Nazi and authoritarian threats. That ethical frame is personal. It does not prove E256 secure or make past and present identical.
scenes.headline: Counter-history, not a security claim
scenes.subhead: Remember the full history. Reverse the symbolism. Build defensively.

scenes.voiceover: The number 256 describes the byte alphabet, from hexadecimal zero-zero through F F. It is a base-256 datapath, not a claim of 256-bit security. The design replaces a 26-letter alphabet, a ten-pair plugboard, a reflector, paper day keys, and odometer stepping. Replacing those features changes the attack surface. It does not measure the new one.
scenes.headline: 256 byte values—not 256 bits of security
scenes.subhead: The alphabet is 00 through FF; the security level is unknown.

scenes.voiceover: Historical attacks used a small alphabet, the reflector's self-encipherment rule, predictable rotor motion, a thin plugboard, and operational key procedures. E256 responds with full-byte permutations, no reflector, four independently enabled rotors, a full 256-entry plugboard, and software-derived message state. These are architectural responses to specific weaknesses. There is no proof that adapted statistical, algebraic, protocol, or physical attacks will fail.
scenes.headline: Patch specific attack conveniences
scenes.subhead: Architecture can answer a requirement; only cryptanalysis can grade the answer.

scenes.voiceover: One byte enters a full 256-entry involutive plugboard and passes forward through four selected rotors. It then combines with a host-derived center-mask byte using exclusive OR. The byte returns through the four inverse rotors and the same plugboard. For one frozen state, the same path decrypts what it encrypted. Nine unique tables require ten serial accesses because the plugboard is visited twice. Reciprocity is a functional invariant, not confidentiality evidence.
scenes.headline: Ten accesses across nine tables
scenes.subhead: Plugboard → four rotors → center mask → four inverse rotors → plugboard

scenes.voiceover: Day material contains one full plugboard and 16 forward-and-reverse rotor pairs. A message nonce selects four active rotors, four starting offsets, a 64-bit state seed, and a center-mask key. Hardware loads only the active plugboard and four rotor pairs: nine tables, or 2,304 bytes. After each accepted byte, a shift register with linear feedback feeds a nonlinear filter. That filter decides independently which of the four rotors step.
scenes.headline: Sixteen rotors in the pool; four active
scenes.subhead: A nonce selects rotors, offsets, state seed, and the center schedule.

scenes.voiceover: The host owns the handshake, key derivation, container authentication, nonce discipline, and center-mask schedule. For each byte, it sends one atomic tuple: payload, center mask, and absolute byte counter. The RTL checks that counter before transforming or advancing state. It does not store the message-authentication key, and it does not derive or validate the mask itself. That trust boundary is explicit and still under audit.
scenes.headline: The hardware trusts a supplied mask
scenes.subhead: The host authenticates and derives; RTL checks the counter and transforms.

scenes.voiceover: The architecture I just described is pinned by a validation receipt, so none of it has to be taken on trust. The identity block names the compatibility key, so a mismatched profile is rejected rather than silently accepted. The state rules are printed as formulas: the conjugated XOR center, and an absolute byte counter that starts at zero. The hardware validates that counter and the directed center, and decryption is checked as reciprocal. Then the byte path, twice. Stream bus and lite bus each carry the same 2,304 bytes of tables and the same 1,024-byte payload. The last screen is the part I care about most. Human review is pending, finding E256-003 is open, and the receipt states in its own text that AI review is not acceptance. This is implementation parity, not a security proof.
scenes.label: PRESERVED RECEIPT · fixture-v4 parity evidence · not a security proof

scenes.voiceover: The update order is part of the cipher identity. First snapshot the tuple and compare its counter. Then transform under the current offsets and emit the output. Only after acceptance does the machine apply the captured four-bit step mask, clock its state register, and increment the counter. A counter mismatch raises an error and must not advance the stream.
scenes.headline: Validate, transform, emit, then step
scenes.subhead: A counter mismatch raises an error and must not advance the stream.

scenes.voiceover: E256 removes or changes several conveniences used against M4. The live fixture has bounded reciprocity and cross-implementation parity receipts. Its security level, comparative strength, and production suitability remain unknown. Use standardized authenticated encryption for real data. Next, we examine the failed generations, the offline promotion loop, and what evidence is still missing.
scenes.headline: A response matrix is not a security proof
scenes.subhead: E256 removes selected M4 conveniences; comparative strength remains unknown.

episodes.title: E256 — Evolution Without Hype
episodes.youtubeTitle: E256 Evolution Without Hype: Autopsy, Offline Promotion, Open Audit
episodes.description: The honest E256 offshoot story: three related but distinct search roles, quarantined v1 failures, immutable runtime profiles, deterministic offline candidate promotion, bounded parity evidence, open threats, and the long-lived-algorithm thought experiment. Experimental; not for real secrets. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: Could a cipher lineage improve after each disclosed weakness? E256 treats that as a research question, not a promise of immortality. The running profile is immutable. Candidate changes happen offline, keep their failed ancestors visible, and require explicit promotion.
scenes.headline: Evolution without hype
scenes.subhead: The research ledger changes. The running cipher does not mutate itself.

scenes.voiceover: Three related projects use search for different jobs. In HELUT's core TensorLUT path, search adjusts continuous truth-table values and may emit a discrete circuit. In the Enigma application, the Bombe searches historical M4 hypotheses and never changes that cipher. In the separate E256 offshoot, profile search proposes a new, versioned construction for later review. Shared optimization tools do not make them one system.
scenes.headline: Core path, application, offshoot
scenes.subhead: TensorLUT genotype · M4 hypothesis · E256 profile

scenes.voiceover: Earlier E256 generations passed their whole test set while hiding structural failures. Their state transition lost rank as it clocked, a sampled fraction of seeds locked at zero, and one nonlinear formula correlated perfectly with a linear input. That last one is the only figure here I can still point at in a retained receipt, where normalized linear correlation reads one against a bound of 0.035. The specific counts I quote for the rest come from development notes whose logs were not kept, so treat them as history rather than evidence. Those profiles and their grades are quarantined. The lesson is not that evolution saved the cipher. It is that implementations can agree while testing the wrong invariant.
scenes.headline: Passing tests hid a collapsing machine
scenes.subhead: Thirty-five checks passed while the old recurrence lost almost all rank.

scenes.voiceover: The live fixture-v4 profile cannot breed or apply mutations at runtime. Red-team pressure is recorded. A deterministic offline search may propose candidates, and it may return no acceptable candidate. Separate holdout attacks and receipt validation come next. Only an explicit human promotion can create a new compatibility identity. Silent fallback to an older profile is forbidden.
scenes.headline: No mutation in the live stream
scenes.subhead: Record pressure → search offline → holdout → validate → human promotion

scenes.voiceover: The live fixture covers 1,024 payload bytes, nine tables, ten traces, and 25 artifacts. Swift, direct RTL, two bus paths, and an internal Rust consumer agree on that fixture. The publication suite reports 49 passing checks, plus one bounded five-part certificate. This is useful implementation evidence. It is not independent cryptanalysis, a confidentiality proof, or an external known-answer test.
scenes.headline: Strong engineering receipts, open cryptography
scenes.subhead: 1,024 bytes · 9 tables · 10 traces · 25 artifacts · same repository boundary

scenes.voiceover: Here is that ladder as a file rather than a slide. Four independent implementations are listed with their own status: the Swift fixture suite, direct RTL, the native nonlinear feedback RTL, and a Rust reference that nobody shares code with. Under the Rust row is the ladder itself: 1,024 bytes of known answers, nine tables, ten trace files, 25 artifacts, and a reciprocal decrypt that passes. Then the formal certificate, which is exactly one test with five named checks, followed by 49 publication guard checks with zero failures. And then the screen I insisted on keeping. The optimizer verdict on this profile is a bounded failure, labelled in the file as not security evidence. Human review is pending and the audit finding is still open. Four agreeing implementations is a strong parity result and a weak security claim.
scenes.label: PRESERVED RECEIPT · four implementations · one row left open

scenes.voiceover: The active audit still carries open construction, protocol, parser, lifecycle, RTL, fault, and side-channel findings. Human acceptance of the center construction remains open. The bus wrappers and table loader need adversarial hardening. No calibrated matrix of standard attacks or independent external implementation exists. Optional timing jitter is not side-channel protection. E256 remains a laboratory, not a product.
scenes.headline: The security case is still open
bullets: Construction and human acceptance
Protocol, parser, replay, and lifecycle
RTL buses, table loading, faults, and side channels
Independent attacks and external implementations

scenes.voiceover: A compromised message cannot be unsent, and a failed profile cannot retroactively protect old traffic. But a disclosed weakness can become evidence for a new, incompatible profile and better future experiments. The question is whether a versioned lineage can survive repeated criticism without hiding its dead ends. That could make the research long-lived. It would not make the algorithm immortal, autonomous, or unbreakable.
scenes.headline: Long-lived lineage—not an immortal cipher
scenes.subhead: A failure can inform a future profile; it cannot protect yesterday's message.

scenes.voiceover: Today, fixture-v4 is the only live public profile. A fixture-v5 lane records staged engineering progress, but it has not been promoted and inherits no security claim. Failed profiles remain visible. Open findings remain open. The living part is the research ledger, not the running cipher. For real secrets, use standardized, reviewed authenticated encryption. Next, the most useful episode in this series: everything that almost worked.

episodes.title: Almost — The Near Misses
episodes.youtubeTitle: Almost: What HELUT Nearly Does, and the Exact Margin It Misses By
episodes.description: The most useful episode: HELUT's capability near misses, sorted by the kind of margin they miss by. One flip-flop short, a few bits short, a pass with no headroom, correct but unproven, one decode short, and two failures that turned out to be measurement bugs. Living research, stated as levers rather than limits. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: The interesting part of a research project is not the list of things that worked. It is the list of things that almost worked, and by exactly how much. This episode walks through HELUT's near misses. Each one is a measured margin with a named lever, because a limit you can measure is a target, and a limit you cannot is just a story.
scenes.headline: Almost
scenes.subhead: Every failure has a margin and a lever.

scenes.voiceover: The sharpest near miss is an encrypted processor tick at full production size. Every one of roughly 2,000 encrypted look-up-table evaluations completes. It takes about half an hour. Then a single flip-flop disagrees with the cleartext answer: it wanted zero and got one. Using a finer encoding did not fix it, and the log names the exact cell that failed. Two other results box it in. The same circuit passes at small size in under two seconds, and a route that shrinks the wire dimension first passes at full size in 114 seconds. So the capability exists. The direct road has one broken cell on it.
scenes.headline: 2,006 agree. One doesn't.
scenes.subhead: It fails at a single named cell.

scenes.voiceover: Most encrypted results are graded against one bar: an error probability of two to the minus sixty-four. Measured against that bar, the margins are thin in both directions. One configuration clears it with about one and a half orders to spare. Another falls short by roughly four, and only a wider spacing recovers it. A third slides off gradually as the wire dimension grows, from comfortably decodable, to marginal, to a single failed decode. None of those are mysteries. They are dials with known positions.
scenes.headline: Thin margins, both ways
scenes.subhead: Some configurations clear it by a hair. Others miss by a hair.

scenes.voiceover: One result is stranger than a failure. A configuration cleared the bar, but its bound tolerated only about five percent growth in measured spread, and the spread actually observed across similar runs was closer to fifty percent. So the result was true as recorded and would not survive ordinary variance. Rather than bank it, the project moved to a wider spacing with more than double the headroom. A pass you cannot lean on is treated here as a near miss, not a win.
scenes.headline: Technically true, not yet trustworthy
scenes.subhead: It clears the bar, but not the noise.

scenes.voiceover: There is a category where the machine gives the right answer and the mathematics has not caught up. At one spacing, encrypted output matched cleartext output on every tested path, while the error estimate swung wildly between trial counts. Correctness passed; the bound was unstable. These are not the same achievement, and collapsing them is how projects start overclaiming. The honest description is that it computes correctly at a setting we cannot yet certify.
scenes.headline: Right, but not proven.
scenes.subhead: Parity passes. The bound stays unstable.

scenes.voiceover: Some near misses are not about size at all. A 58-gate encrypted slice of the E256 cipher passes at full production size on one encoding path, in about 23 seconds. On the neighbouring encoding it fails outright. The same is true of an adder at one particular setting. Nothing about the circuit changed. Only the numerical route did. That tells you the boundary lives in the encoding, which is a much more useful thing to know than a general shrug about scale.
scenes.headline: Same circuit, adjacent encoding, different verdict
scenes.subhead: One route passes. Its neighbour fails.
scenes.kicker: Right on one path, wrong on its sibling

scenes.voiceover: One near miss is purely economic. To pin down one error figure to within a single order of magnitude would take tens of thousands of trials, roughly a week and a half of continuous compute. To demonstrate that the same figure clears the bar takes about two dozen. Those are different questions with wildly different prices, and noticing that was worth more than any hardware upgrade. The capability was never in doubt. The affordable evidence was.
scenes.headline: Clearing a bar is cheaper than measuring a value
scenes.subhead: Clear it: ~24 trials. Resolve it: ~35,000.

scenes.voiceover: On the TensorLUT side, the proof ladder is short and honest. One fully observed look-up table is proved. A two-table cascade is proved and emits hardware. Arbitrary networks are open. The penalty strength needed to force values binary was measured at about three point seven three on the small case, bracketing a crossover observed between two and four. Then came the useful embarrassment: that threshold is a known result from nineteen sixty-nine, rediscovered. What genuinely remains open is how it scales with depth and fan-out.
scenes.headline: One table proved. Two tables proved. Then open.
scenes.subhead: The threshold was published in 1969.

scenes.voiceover: Two entries were not near misses at all. A clean-looking encrypted failure was traced to encrypting inputs in randomized dictionary order while drawing from one shared random stream, so different wires received mismatched masks. Sorting the loops fixed it, the failure was withdrawn, and a guard now protects it. A plausible physical explanation had already been written down before the real cause surfaced. The same bug had made another row flaky; it now passes four times out of four. And going the other way, seven timing rows had understated the code by about a factor of two. The ledger was wrong in both directions.
scenes.headline: Two failures that were measurement bugs
bullets: A withdrawn encrypted failure: randomized iteration order
A flaky row that became four-for-four after the fix
Seven timing rows that had understated the code by ~2×

scenes.voiceover: This is that guard, running. It is worth watching in real time because the bug it catches was invisible by design. Swift reseeds its dictionary hash ordering on every process launch. The encrypted path was iterating primary inputs in dictionary order while drawing from one shared random stream, so the masks a wire received depended on where the hash seed happened to land that run. On thin decode margins that turns a correct answer into a coin toss, and it cost a real claim: an n=512 covering adder was filed as a noise failure and later withdrawn, because the failure was in the harness rather than the mathematics. The fix was to sort the loops. The guard is the interesting part. It runs the same work in 5 completely separate processes, fingerprints each one, and demands all 5 agree. If hash ordering still leaked into the result, these lines would differ. Watch them arrive one at a time. Five processes, one fingerprint, PASS. And this gate was itself tested by putting the bug back: 3 distinct fingerprints across 6 processes, which is how you know the gate can actually fail.
scenes.label: LIVE RUN · recorded 2026-09-05 · the guard that closed the withdrawn failure

scenes.voiceover: One result belongs here precisely because it is nowhere near. Melting an entire 925-gate sequential cipher from a cold start shatters: around 14,000 values refuse to settle, and a related attempt on a live cipher cone ends with more than 1,200 still stuck between zero and one. That is not a margin, it is a wall. Including it is what makes the thin margins credible. A project where everything is almost working is not reporting carefully.
scenes.headline: Not everything is close
scenes.subhead: A cold-start melt of 925 gates shatters.

scenes.voiceover: Every episode here carries a date for one reason: this is living research on living silicon, and the ledger is expected to move. episodes.title: The Encrypted Processor
episodes.youtubeTitle: Running a RISC-V Core Under Encryption: One Tick at a Time
episodes.description: HELUT's deepest result: a PicoRV32 RISC-V core evaluated under torus FHE. The demo-size ladder from one tick to a store-then-load program, the two levers that cut the cost, one encrypted tick at production polynomial size, the extract-and-key-switch route, and the bounded non-claims. Not Linux, not a production encrypted CPU. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: A processor is just a circuit. So if HELUT can evaluate circuits under encryption, it should be able to run a processor under encryption. It can. This episode is the ladder from a single encrypted clock cycle to a small program that stores a value in memory and reads it back, without the machine ever seeing that value in the clear.
scenes.headline: The encrypted processor
scenes.subhead: A circuit that runs a program it cannot see.

scenes.voiceover: That is PicoRV32, a real RISC-V core, not a teaching example. Yosys mapped it to 2,006 lookup tables and 1,565 flip-flops, and the flip-flops are the hard part, because state has to survive every tick. Now it runs encrypted, and the decrypted result is compared against a clear oracle. Result: PASS, one row, about 176 milliseconds. Then read the two lines above that verdict, because those are the honest ones. Classical bits, 32, and the harness prints its own answer to whether that clears 128: no. The bootstrap key is an exact-noiseless construction. So this is a real processor computing correctly on encrypted state at a demonstration parameter, not a secure one.
scenes.label: LIVE RUN · recorded 2026-09-05 · N=64 CPU · demonstration parameter, not production

scenes.voiceover: The processor is PicoRV32, a compact RISC-V core that other people use in real designs. Synthesized down to two-input look-up tables it becomes 4,785 tables and 1,565 flip-flops. Re-synthesized to six-input tables it drops to 2,006 tables, a 58 percent cut, with the same flip-flop count. Those flip-flops are the interesting part. They hold state between clock ticks, which means the encrypted circuit has memory.
scenes.headline: A real RISC-V core
scenes.subhead: 2,006 look-up tables and 1,565 flip-flops.

scenes.voiceover: One encrypted clock tick at demonstration size took 76 milliseconds. That number comes with a hard caveat. At that size the encryption parameters carry about four bits of hardness, and four bits is not security. It is a functional test. The point of a demonstration size is to prove the semantics are right, cheaply, before paying for production parameters.
scenes.headline: One tick, 76 milliseconds
scenes.subhead: Four bits of hardness is a functional test.

scenes.voiceover: Then it stops being a single tick. A scripted reset holds the core low for three cycles and releases it, and the encrypted core boots across ten ticks. Given a read-only memory full of no-op instructions, the program counter walks: ten fetches, at addresses zero, four, eight, and on up to hexadecimal twenty-four. Then a real program. Load the number one into a register, store that register to memory, and load it back. The store writes with all four byte-enables set and a value of one. The later load reads one. The circuit executed a program it could not see.
scenes.headline: It executed a program it could not read
scenes.subhead: The store wrote a 1. The later load read a 1.

scenes.voiceover: Most of the work here was not cryptography. It was flip-flop semantics. A plain D flip-flop must not refresh its incoming data the way a look-up table output does, and 91 cells were doing exactly that. The synthesis tool emits flip-flops where the clock enable gates the reset, and that has to be modelled exactly or the boot sequence diverges. Read data has to be held for the cycle the core actually samples it. This is the unglamorous half of making an encrypted circuit agree with a cleartext one.
scenes.headline: Most of the work was flip-flop semantics
bullets: 91 cells refreshed data they should not have
Clock enable gates the reset—model it exactly
Read data must be held for the sampled cycle

scenes.voiceover: Two changes moved the cost more than any parameter tuning. Re-synthesizing to six-input look-up tables cut the table count by 58 percent. Then the scheduler learned to evaluate every ready table in a tick concurrently, even when the circuit contains flip-flops, and to skip tables that are only an identity or a constant. On this core that was about an eight-fold speed-up: 1.35 seconds down to 0.165.
scenes.headline: Fewer tables, and a smarter schedule
scenes.subhead: 58% fewer tables, then ~8x faster.

scenes.voiceover: With those levers, one encrypted tick of the whole processor ran at production polynomial size: 373.89 seconds, just over six minutes, for a single clock cycle. Re-measured three times, the spread was two tenths of one percent. The hardness figure printed for that configuration is about 176 bits, and it carries its own caveat: it agrees with the reference estimator on some parameter sets and disagrees on others, so it is not a blanket security level.
scenes.headline: Six minutes for one clock cycle
scenes.subhead: 373.89 seconds, stable to two tenths of a percent.

scenes.voiceover: There is a catch. Under the noisier encoding needed for deeper work, the direct route at full native dimension fails. Every combinational table completes, and then a single flip-flop disagrees. The fix was not a bigger machine. Extracting the sample and switching it down to a much smaller wire dimension first, sixty-four instead of 1,024, makes it pass: one tick in 114 seconds, the ten-tick boot in about nineteen minutes, and the instruction fetch in about fifteen. Truncating that extraction instead of properly key-switching it would be unsound, which is exactly why the honest route is the slower one.
scenes.headline: Shrink the wire
scenes.subhead: One tick in 114 s. A boot in ~19 minutes.

scenes.voiceover: What this is not. It is not Linux, and it is not a production encrypted processor. The demonstration-size results carry four bits of hardness, which is a functional check and nothing more. The production-size results are single ticks and short tick counts, not workloads. A load instruction under the noisier encoding at full native dimension is still open. Every one of those sentences sits in the ledger, directly beside the results.
scenes.headline: What this is not
bullets: Not Linux · not a production encrypted CPU
Demo-size results carry 4 bits of hardness
Single ticks and short runs, not workloads

scenes.voiceover: An encrypted processor tick costs about 114 seconds. The cleartext search campaign in this series runs 37.4 million circuit settings per second. Those two numbers come from the same compiler and must never be mixed. The distance between them is the real research frontier, and it is where the next levers have to come from. Next, the wider set of problems this substrate has actually been pointed at.
scenes.headline: The gap is the frontier
scenes.subhead: 114 s per encrypted tick vs 37.4M settings/s.

episodes.title: The Application Gallery
episodes.youtubeTitle: What HELUT Has Actually Been Pointed At: Radio, Regex, Trees, Ciphers
episodes.description: The breadth of HELUT applications, organized around the distinction that matters most: the same netlist runs in an oracle shape-laboratory tier and an encrypted tier, and only one of them is FHE. Covers the GNU Radio matcher, regex versus decision tree, encrypted sequential circuits, carry-save architecture, the Mulein width sweep where sixteen lanes lose to four, and the Python-only toy cipher. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: HELUT has been pointed at more than one problem. A radio receiver, a regular-expression matcher, a decision tree, a processor, and a historical cipher search. This episode is that gallery. But it is organized around one distinction, because it is the easiest thing in this project to get wrong: most of these circuits run in two different tiers, and only one of those tiers is encrypted.
scenes.headline: The same circuit, twice
scenes.subhead: Breadth is easy. Labelling the tier is not.

scenes.voiceover: Start with the demo that needs no explanation. That circuit began as Verilog. Yosys mapped it to lookup tables, and HELUT loaded the netlist. It has no string-search function anywhere in it. First it announces its own shape: the module, 3 input ports over 24 bits, 1 output bit, then checks itself against a known answer and passes. Then bytes go in one at a time. Watch the right-hand column. The match bit fires at byte 10, which is the F in DEFCON, and again at byte 23. Nothing else moves. Last screen, the honest half: give it a stream containing none of the three bytes it knows and nothing fires at all. A detector that always says yes is not a detector. This is the clear Boolean path, no antenna, nothing intercepted, and it is a fixed three-byte literal rather than a general pattern engine.
scenes.label: LIVE RUN · recorded 2026-09-05 · clear Boolean oracle · no antenna

scenes.voiceover: Start with the demo that needs no explanation. A GNU Radio flowgraph generates a baseband signal, adds noise, and recovers bytes. Those bytes feed a Yosys netlist compiled from Verilog: a three-character regular-expression matcher. When the letters D, E, F arrive, the circuit flags a match. No antenna is involved and nothing is intercepted; it is a closed loop on one machine. The same demo then runs 10,000 windows as a batch to show throughput, and finally freezes a single window under encryption at demonstration size, where being slow is the entire point.
scenes.headline: Matching bytes off a signal
scenes.subhead: Baseband, noise, recovered bytes, then a netlist.

scenes.voiceover: Here is the distinction. The same netlist can run on two different backends. In the oracle tier, values are ordinary numbers, the batch can be enormous, and it runs in real time. That tier proves the shape of the computation: the wiring, the clocking, the batch axis. In the encrypted tier, the wires carry lattice samples and every look-up table costs a blind rotation. Same circuit, same answers, wildly different cost, and wildly different claims. Calling the oracle tier encrypted computing is the most common error available here, and it is the one this project guards hardest.
scenes.headline: Two backends, one netlist
scenes.subhead: Shape laboratory versus encrypted evaluation.

scenes.voiceover: Two of the shape-laboratory demos tried to graduate into the encrypted tier. The regular-expression matcher made it: 23 look-up tables, evaluated encrypted at production polynomial size, in about 27 seconds. The decision tree did not. It still runs only at demonstration size, and its covering path on Metal remains open. Same family, same compiler, one graduated and one is still waiting. That difference is recorded rather than smoothed over.
scenes.headline: One graduated. One did not.
scenes.subhead: Regex reached production size. The tree is still waiting.

scenes.voiceover: Encrypted state also works at production size, as long as the circuit stays small. A four-bit counter passes in about 16 seconds across four stimuli. A toy instruction set with a no-op and an add passes in about 20 seconds. A single round of the E256 cipher, 58 gates wide, passes in about 23 seconds. None of those is a processor, and none of them touches live memory. They are the stepping stones between an encrypted adder and the encrypted processor from the last episode.
scenes.headline: The stepping stones
scenes.subhead: Counter, toy instruction set, one cipher round.

scenes.voiceover: One result is a useful corrective. A four-bit adder was synthesized two ways: a ripple-carry version at 11 look-up tables, and a carry-save version at eight. That is a 27 percent cut, and both versions pass the correctness gate. The lesson is that the cheapest win available here came from choosing a better circuit architecture, not from any search or optimizer. The ledger labels it explicitly as architecture, and not as a TensorLUT melt.
scenes.headline: The cheapest win was a better circuit
scenes.subhead: Carry-save against ripple-carry: 11 tables down to 8.

scenes.voiceover: Now the result I did not expect. The cleartext Enigma search engine can be built with one, two, four, eight, or sixteen parallel lanes. Sixteen lanes cost sixteen times the silicon: about 758,000 look-up tables against 45,000 for a single lane. Every width produces a byte-identical result digest, so it is provably the same computation. And sixteen lanes are slower than one: 231 complete receipts per second against 234. Four lanes win, at 276. Width four was selected on measured throughput, not on size, not on synthesis time, and not on intuition.
scenes.headline: Sixteen lanes lose to four
scenes.subhead: Same digest every width. Wider is not faster.

scenes.voiceover: The subsystem around that engine has deliberately memorable names, and they encode a real distinction. A transcript can be wrong in two different ways, and conflating them causes bad science. If a recorded letter is merely suspect, that is edge-erasure tolerance, handled by the Tolerant Closure, informally the Garble Blaster 9000. If letters are missing or extra, the whole rotor alignment shifts, which is splice geometry, handled by the Splice Engine, informally the Indel Blaster 9000. Different fault, different repair, separate receipts. A survivor from either one is a repair hypothesis, not a result.
scenes.headline: Garble and Indel
scenes.subhead: A suspect letter is not the same as a missing one.

scenes.voiceover: Not everything here needs Apple silicon. A reviewer asked a sharp question: show two ciphers of the same type, one sound and one broken on purpose, then demonstrate telling them apart. The answer runs on nothing but Python. One substitution-permutation skeleton, built twice: once with a real S-box, and once with an invertible affine one that looks fine and is not. Four separate tests distinguish them, including a difference table that reads four against sixteen, and key recovery from a single known pair with no search at all. It is the smallest honest example in the project, and it is deliberately not a claim row.
scenes.headline: Two ciphers, one broken on purpose
scenes.subhead: The on-ramp for anyone without Apple silicon.

scenes.voiceover: One pairing keeps this gallery honest. The cleartext search engine delivers about 276 complete receipts per second. An encrypted processor tick costs about 114 seconds. Both come out of the same compiler, and putting them in one sentence as though they were comparable is exactly the error this series is built to avoid. Everything here carries a date, and the gallery grows when the receipts do. More MuleinLabs work is coming, on this and on other things entirely.
scenes.headline: Two numbers, one firewall
scenes.subhead: 276 receipts/s cleartext · 114 s per encrypted tick.
