episodes.title: Why It Holds
episodes.youtubeTitle: We Handed the Machine the Answer and It Walked Away: Why P1030680 Holds
episodes.description: A measured correction to why P1030680 remains unbroken. The August sparse-model receipt is preserved as history: 4 of 72 letters and 0 of 10 plugs. The independently attested dense bigram table moved the same known-shell control to 21 of 72 and 4 of 10. Objective v1 reached 25 of 72 and 5 of 10, but normalized the full attack score with raw-bigram moments; objective v2 calibrates the exact attack score and its paired trigram relationship. V1 and v2 recover the same candidate, the IC-only rank remains 223,118 of 456,976, and every checkpoint remains NO BREAK. The final assessment is a separate fail-closed policy gate, not a claim of statistical independence. Current target-length generic/naval rows and the oracle plug-seeding ladder are shown as objective-independent controls from sealed deterministic receipts. P1030680 remains unbroken. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: An earlier cut gave a clean answer for why P1030680 still holds: the hardware was fast enough, but the scorer could not recognise the right answer even when it started there. That diagnosis survived. The sparse bigram table was a real wiring defect, and repairing it moved the known-key rehearsal substantially. Then the first repaired objective failed its own calibration audit: it standardized the complete attack score with raw-bigram statistics. Objective v2 fixes that error and recovers the same candidate. This episode preserves every stage, puts the correction beside it, and refuses to turn better coordinates into a victory. The target still has no key and no plaintext.
scenes.headline: Why it holds
scenes.subhead: A real defect moved the numbers. Its calibration audit moved the model—not the verdict.

scenes.voiceover: The test is straightforward. Take a different message from the same network on the same day, one whose key was published decades ago, and truncate it to 72 letters, the exact length of the unsolved target. Then grade the pipeline in layers. First, can the index-of-coincidence sieve rank the true message key? Second, if we skip the search and start on the true rotor setting, can the plugboard climb stay near the answer? Third, does a separate fail-closed final assessment accept the recovered text? Those are different questions, but they are not claimed to be statistically independent evidence streams. Keeping the roles separate is what made the defects visible.
scenes.headline: Give the machine a message you can check
scenes.subhead: A published key, truncated to the target's length.

scenes.voiceover: First check. Hand the machine the correct wheels and rings, so the only unknown is the message key, and rank all 456,976 candidates by index of coincidence. The true key is number 223,118: the top 48.825 percent, statistically the middle of the pile. That number is identical in the sparse run, the dense-table probe, superseded objective v1, and current objective v2, because this first level uses only index of coincidence. It is our internal control. The language-model and calibration repairs did not quietly change the sieve, and the sieve still has no useful signal at 72 letters.
scenes.headline: The true key still ranks dead centre
scenes.subhead: 223,118 of 456,976 · unchanged by every scorer repair

scenes.voiceover: Now skip the search and start directly on the true rotor setting. The preserved August scorer recovered four letters out of 72 and no true plugs. Wiring in the dense bigram table moved it to 21 letters and four true plugs. Objective v1 moved recovery again, to 25 letters and five of ten true plugs, with seven proposed. Its calibration was still wrong: the full bigram, index-of-coincidence, and crib attack score had been normalized with raw-bigram moments. Objective v2 calibrates that exact attack score and its paired trigram relationship. It changes the objective coordinates but recovers the same 25-letter, five-plug candidate. All four checkpoints remain visibly incomplete, and the separate fail-closed final assessment prints NO BREAK.
scenes.headline: The repair moved the climb; v2 fixed its calibration
scenes.subhead: 4 → 21 → 25 → 25 letters. Every row still says NO BREAK.
scenes.kicker: Check two · sparse, dense, v1, v2

scenes.voiceover: This is the original sparse-model receipt. It is staying in the episode because corrections should preserve the before state, not erase it. The control, true key, and 72-letter length are printed at the top. Level one lands at rank 223,118. Level two recovers four letters and zero true plugs. Level three prints NO BREAK and the old diagnostic name, likeness. Those are authentic August results, but they are no longer the current scorer result. Read this footage as the baseline that exposed the problem. The next receipt shows the dense probe, superseded objective v1, and current objective v2 side by side.
scenes.label: HISTORICAL RECEIPT · August sparse model · preserved, not relabeled

scenes.voiceover: Here is the current correction, played from sealed receipts rather than recomputed for the camera. The first screen fixes the four-step chronology: four letters and zero plugs under the sparse August model; 21 and four with the dense table; 25 and five under superseded objective v1; and the same 25 and five under current objective v2. V2 changes the recovered candidate's objective from 5.9117 to 6.7292 and the truth coordinate from 6.8812 to 7.7110. The invariant level-one rank remains 223,118. Bigram position equals 1.08 is a diagnostic coordinate, not probability or confidence. The separate fail-closed final assessment still says NO BREAK.
scenes.label: CURRENT RECEIPT · sealed playback · sparse → dense → v1 → v2

scenes.voiceover: The finding is now more precise. The first-level sieve is still statistically blind. The second-level climb was handicapped first by a sparse bigram table. Objective v1 then combined attack and trigram evidence but calibrated the complete bigram, index-of-coincidence, and crib attack score with raw-bigram moments and used raw-bigram-to-trigram correlation. Objective v2 calibrates the exact attack-score population and its paired trigram correlation on the same frozen 400 controls. Python and Ruby auditors agree bit for bit, and Swift locks those values in regression tests. Publication then uses a separate policy gate with Core structure checks and the exact hash-bound trigram model. It fails closed if trigram evidence is unavailable. Better ranking is not promoted into confidence, and no claim of statistical independence is made.
scenes.headline: Ranking improved; assessment stayed fail-closed
bullets: IC-only rank unchanged: 223,118 / 456,976
Objective v1 and v2: same 25/72, 5/10 candidate
Separate fail-closed final assessment: NO BREAK

scenes.voiceover: There is also a crib-free attack that climbs the plugboard at candidate rotor settings and ranks the resulting scores. This legacy staged benchmark does not consume the Enigma search objective, so it is a control rather than evidence that objective v2 changed the ladder. The August curve crossed zero at about 200 letters; that remains a historical baseline, not a newly measured current threshold. The current rerun sampled 72, 100, 140, 180, and 252 letters. At the target length the generic model wins five of 30 controls and its median margin is minus 0.2306. The published 78-letter record and the 72-letter target remain the challenge; the current target row is still negative.
scenes.headline: The 72-letter margin stays negative
scenes.subhead: Historical crossing ≈200; current target row −0.2306.

scenes.voiceover: The audit has three steps. First, replace the 10,359-letter historical bigram sample with the 28.5-million-letter fixture that was already present. The old table put 235 of 676 cells on one finite smoothing floor; the dense table observes 674 cells and leaves only J X and Q Y there. Python, Ruby, and Swift agree on those dense scores bit for bit. Second, objective v1 combines standardized evidence with the exact trigram model and moves recovery from 21 letters to 25. Third, inspect what was actually standardized. The numerator was the complete attack score, including the bigram score, distance from the index-of-coincidence target, and configured crib matches, but v1 used raw-bigram moments. Objective v2 calibrates the exact attack score and its paired trigram relationship. It recovers the same candidate with corrected coordinates. The August claim that partial exhaustion closed 68 percent belongs only to that sparse-model A B test; it has not been rerun here.
scenes.headline: Fix the data path, then calibrate the whole attack
scenes.subhead: 4 → 21 → 25 → 25 letters; still NO BREAK.

scenes.voiceover: The oracle-seeded ladder was rerun with the objective-v2 binary, but its staged scorer does not consume the Enigma search objective, so every stdout receipt is byte-identical to the v1-binary bundle. With no oracle plugs, the 72-letter median margin is minus 0.1226. Seed four genuinely correct plugs at the true setting and four random plugs at each decoy, and the median flips to plus 0.3308, with six of ten plugs and 47 percent of letters recovered. Seed eight and all ten controls recover all ten plugs and all plaintext, at plus 1.0488. Those plugs come from the known key. This proves a true Bombe stop carrying enough correct plug structure is finishable. It does not find that stop or break P1030680.
scenes.headline: A true stop is still finishable
scenes.subhead: K=4: +0.3308. K=8: complete recovery.

scenes.voiceover: The naval-dialect hypothesis was reasonable and remains worth recording precisely. Naval traffic uses X and Y as punctuation, spells numbers, and repeats procedure markers. But at 72 letters the current generic model wins five of 30 controls with a median margin of minus 0.2306, while the leave-one-out naval model wins four with minus 0.2496. Slightly worse, not a rescue. At 252 letters both already win every control, and naval improves the positive margin from plus 0.9273 to plus 1.1531. Like the seed ladder, this staged A B command does not consume the Enigma search objective; its v2-binary output is byte-identical to v1. The generic corpus is not wrong data: it powers the dense bigrams and generic trigram model.
scenes.headline: Naval German does not rescue 72 letters

scenes.voiceover: These are current binary-bound controls, again played from sealed text. The generic and leave-one-out naval tables show the 72-letter failure and the already-winning 252-letter case side by side. The second table walks oracle seeds from zero through eight plugs. The sign flips at four. Every generic, naval, and seed stdout hash exactly matches the preceding v1-binary bundle because these legacy staged scorers do not consume the Enigma search objective. That is a dependency boundary, not evidence that objective v2 changed these rows. The final screen states the claim boundary: ranking benchmark, not publication verdict; oracle upper bound, not a way to find a stop. P1030680 still has no key, plaintext, or break.
scenes.label: CURRENT RECEIPT · objective-v2 binary controls · ranking only

scenes.voiceover: So what remains after fixing the wire and calibrating the full attack score? First, the index-of-coincidence sieve still puts the true message key in the middle. An all-setting climb can avoid that sieve, but it must separate truth from a vast population of fitted noise. Second, the objective-v2 known-shell candidate is better than the sparse baseline but incomplete: 25 letters and five true plugs are not a readable message, and the separate fail-closed assessment correctly rejects it. Third, the strongest measured lever assumes information we do not possess. Four oracle-correct plugs flip the sign, but the target needs a real Bombe stop to supply them. The next improvement has to move one of those measured boundaries. More corpus wiring is no longer the answer, and a high bigram position is not evidence by itself.
scenes.headline: The defect was real. So is the remaining wall.
bullets: IC rank is unchanged: the first-level sieve still misses truth
Objective v2 reaches 25/72 and 5/10, then fails closed
Next lever: real Bombe-forced plugs, not oracle plugs

scenes.voiceover: The correction leaves three numbers any future idea has to move: the unchanged rank of 223,118, the current 25 recovered letters, and five recovered plugs. Or it has to replace oracle seeds with structure from a real stop. An improvement that moves none of those is decoration. P1030680 remains unbroken. The August sparse receipt and superseded v1 evidence remain visible, while the objective-v2 receipt sits beside them with corrected calibration and the same candidate. That is what a defect should do to a living research narrative: change the coordinates, narrow the explanation, preserve provenance, and leave the verdict exactly where the evidence puts it.
scenes.headline: Three numbers are the gate
scenes.subhead: 223,118 · 25/72 · 5/10 · and still NO BREAK

episodes.title: The Frontier
episodes.youtubeTitle: Five Wild Ideas, and the Small Experiment That Would Earn Each One
episodes.description: The speculative end of HELUT, handled honestly. Five frontier avenues — an encrypted prompt-injection firewall, self-mutating encrypted binaries, encrypted honey-token ledgers, software that evolves its own circuits, and power analysis against FHE as deployed — each paired with the modest first experiment that would earn it a claim row. Includes the dual-use material and the trajectory items. Nothing here is a claim. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: Every episode so far has stuck to things with receipts. This one deliberately does not. It covers the speculative end of the project: the ideas that are exciting, unproven, and in one case explicitly refused. But each one comes with something that keeps it honest. For every wild idea, the repository also names the small, dull experiment that would earn it a place in the ledger. That pairing is the whole episode, because the difference between a frontier and a fantasy is knowing what your next experiment is.
scenes.headline: The frontier
scenes.subhead: Wild ideas are cheap. Next steps are not.

scenes.voiceover: The project sorts every public sentence into one of four boxes. A reproducible claim can be cited and re-run by someone else. An open hedge can be discussed, but the asterisk travels with it. A non-implication is something you must actively stop people concluding. And then there is the frontier: material that is not a claim at all until it earns a reproduce command. The teaching guidance for these is blunt. Do not lecture them as fact, and never put them in a true-or-false question. Everything after this scene lives in that fourth box.
scenes.headline: How speculation gets filed
bullets: Reproducible claim — you may cite it
Open hedge — keep the asterisk
Non-implication — actively prevent the inference
Frontier — never a fact, ever

scenes.voiceover: First idea. Prompt injection against language models is currently fought with other language models and brittle instructions. Suppose instead you evolved a small logic-gate firewall that sits between an untrusted prompt and a local model, and evaluates entirely in the encrypted domain, mutating its own gate topology based on the attacks it successfully blocked. Neither the prompt, nor the weights, nor the defence rules ever appear in the clear. Now the graduating experiment, and notice how much smaller it is: a four-gate encrypted classifier passing a correctness check on synthetic token bits, with a certificate. That comes before any talk of evolution or actual language models.
scenes.headline: A firewall that never sees the prompt
scenes.subhead: First experiment: four gates and a certificate.

scenes.voiceover: Second idea, and the uncomfortable one. An encrypted processor already boots. What happens if you feed it a program that rewrites its own instructions while staying encrypted? The host would see uniform tensor arithmetic while, inside, code mutates and executes where the operating system cannot inspect, debug, or breakpoint it. The repository describes that honestly as malware-class self-modification running inside an accelerator built for privacy, and then does something better than getting excited: it lists claiming this as an explicit non-goal. The graduating experiment is deliberately mundane. An encrypted instruction fetch on a toy machine smaller than the processor we already ran, accompanied by a written ethics note. It is framed as a privacy-architecture question, not as malware homework.
scenes.headline: Code that rewrites itself in the dark
scenes.subhead: Listed as an explicit non-goal, on purpose.
scenes.kicker: Avenue two · refused as a claim

scenes.voiceover: Third idea. Take the batched pattern matcher and put it inside a distributed ledger, so that every time a node synchronises, a large document set is checked against many attacker patterns in a single encrypted pass. If someone queries the store, the store evaluates an encrypted trap and changes state across the mesh, without the storage node learning which file was searched or which trigger fired. The graduating experiment has a twist I like a great deal. Run the pattern matcher at a modest batch with an explicit written non-claim that the node learns nothing, and then go and measure what the host process can still see anyway: message lengths, timings. Honesty before mesh networks.
scenes.headline: A wire it cannot read
scenes.subhead: Then measure what the host still sees.

scenes.voiceover: Fourth idea. Rather than writing a circuit by hand and synthesizing it, mutate the truth tables and the connections directly, then compile the result into a running graph. Taken to its conclusion, a machine meeting an unfamiliar data stream would evolve a custom circuit for it, compile that circuit in seconds, and process the stream through hardware it had just invented. The graduating experiment is one offline generation producing a two-gate circuit that matches a fixed specification, with the wall-clock time for synthesis and lowering written down. No claims about doing it on the fly.
scenes.headline: Software that invents its own hardware
scenes.subhead: One circuit, offline, with a stopwatch.

scenes.voiceover: Fifth idea, and the genuinely adversarial one. Homomorphic evaluation is supposed to look like featureless tensor arithmetic from outside. So point a power meter at the actual graph while it runs controlled inputs, align the traces to circuit ticks rather than wall-clock, and ask whether key-dependent structure still leaks through the energy trace. That would be side-channel analysis against encryption as it is really deployed on a GPU, not against a textbook circuit. The guardrails are written down and they are strict: live graphs only, controlled fixtures only, and tick synchronisation is mandatory. No opportunistic capture of other people's workloads. The graduating experiment is almost comically modest: build the harness, emit the tick markers, and publish a log that says no analysis yet. And note the framing — a clean negative is also a result, because it hardens the claim that the graph is power-flat.
scenes.headline: Encrypted, but still radiating?
scenes.subhead: Live graphs only. Controlled fixtures only.

scenes.voiceover: There is a dual-use edge here that deserves saying out loud rather than hinting at. The machinery that melts a truth table does not care what the circuit is for. Two named legacy stream ciphers sit on the roadmap as candidates: one from early mobile telephony, one from early web encryption. Compiling them to circuits and melting their internal state logic would suggest that differentiable hardware can dismantle late twentieth-century telecommunications cryptography about as readily as it handles 1940s machines. The roadmap carries that idea with a parenthesis attached: not a claim until it is graded and reproducible. Which is the correct place for it, and also the reason to talk about it in public rather than quietly.
scenes.headline: The same tool points backwards
scenes.subhead: Trajectory only. Not a claim until graded.

scenes.voiceover: Beyond the five avenues there is a longer horizon, and the roadmap is careful with it. Point the same continuous-to-discrete engine at the gates that make encrypted computation expensive, and you might find shallower arrangements. Point it at the enormous circuits behind zero-knowledge proofs, and fewer gates with less depth would directly relieve the main bottleneck in private infrastructure. Point it at post-quantum lattice structures, and the ambition gets larger still. Every one of those sentences ends the same way in the source: trajectory only, until receipts exist. Which is exactly how far I am willing to say it here.
scenes.headline: The far end, labelled as far
bullets: Shallower circuits for encrypted gates
Smaller circuits for zero-knowledge proofs
Post-quantum lattice structures

scenes.voiceover: The project sets rules for talking about any of this, and they are worth stealing. Label every paragraph as either frontier or first experiment, so nobody can quote you out of context. Name the specific claim the idea would become if it worked. Name the false conclusion it must not invite along the way. And the test that does the most work: if you cannot even imagine what the evidence would look like, the idea is not ready to be written down as a proposal, let alone announced.
scenes.headline: What earns a frontier idea its place
bullets: Label it: frontier, or first experiment
Name the claim it would become
Name the false conclusion it must not invite
If you cannot imagine the evidence, it is not ready

scenes.voiceover: Five ideas, and not one of them is a result. What makes them frontier rather than fantasy is that each arrived with a specific, small, testable next step, and in one case with a refusal to pursue it as a claim at all. If any of them graduates, it will do so quietly, through a log file and a reproduce command, and this series will say so with a date on it. Next time, something completely different. We stop describing and start building: a circuit written from scratch, on camera, running on data it cannot see.
scenes.headline: Frontier, not fantasy
scenes.subhead: Every idea here arrived with its own next step.

episodes.title: Five Ballots, One Bit
episodes.youtubeTitle: We Built a Private Majority Circuit and Ran It Encrypted on Metal
episodes.description: A from-scratch HELUT experiment with dated terminal receipts: five encrypted ballot bits enter a synthesized majority circuit and one decision bit leaves. Yosys maps the design to three lookup-table cells; all 32 inputs pass clear and demonstration-size encrypted equivalence; and two deterministic endpoints pass at N=1024 on Metal. The initial pre-script run recorded 0.0089 seconds at N=16 and 2.7189 seconds at N=1024; a literal filmed rerun recorded 0.0095 and 2.5320 seconds. Both passed, but two observations are not a timing distribution. The harness owns the key, and the bootstrap-key construction is exact-noiseless, so this is neither a deployed voting protocol nor a noisy-key proof. A closing coda sends the same compiler path through a RISC-V processor instead: 4,785 lookup tables and 1,565 flip-flops running a three-instruction program, padded with no-ops, encrypted on CPU for 48 ticks, all rows matching the clear model at 4.0 modeled classical bits, where the host implements memory and therefore sees addresses and data. Reproduce paths and hashes included. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: Last episode promised that we would stop describing and start building. This is that build. A circuit with five ballot bits as inputs and one bit as output: did at least three voters say yes? I wrote it, synthesized it, exercised every possible input through the clear and encrypted demonstration paths, and then moved the same netlist to a production-parameter-size Metal run. The experiment came before this script. The authored panels use that first dated receipt. Later, you will also see a literal terminal rerun with its own dated values. We keep the two observations separate.
scenes.headline: Five ballots. One bit.
scenes.subhead: The experiment came before the script; the filmed rerun came after.

scenes.voiceover: The boundary comes first. Five ballot bits are encrypted before evaluation. The synthesized circuit computes whether at least three are one. Afterward, the benchmark harness decrypts the single proposal-passes bit inside the process and compares it with a clear golden model. That is the experiment's privacy contract. It is not a voting system. There is no ballot authentication, independent key custody, threshold decryption, coercion resistance, or malicious-party protocol here. The same harness owns the key and performs the comparison. The bounded claim is simply that this circuit can compute on encrypted ballot bits while revealing only the result chosen for decryption.
scenes.headline: Reveal the decision, not five ballots
scenes.subhead: Encrypted inputs in · one decrypted result out

scenes.voiceover: The source is deliberately ordinary Verilog. Zero-extend each vote, add the five bits into a three-bit count, and set proposal-passes when that count is at least three. There is no special voting primitive and no handwritten encrypted algorithm. HELUT needs a circuit, so we give it the simplest readable description of the function we want. The source lives in the hardware examples with its own hash, and its comments carry the limitation beside the code: this demonstrates the shape of private computation, not the rest of a secure election.
scenes.headline: The circuit, from scratch
scenes.subhead: Five one-bit inputs. Sum. Compare with three.

scenes.voiceover: In the initial pre-script run, I ran Yosys 0.68 with ABC allowed to use lookup tables of up to four inputs. It mapped the majority function to three table cells: two with three inputs and one with four. The check pass reported zero problems. That is a mapping result, not a proof that three is mathematically minimal. The separate endpoint receipt says all-zero ballots reject and all-one ballots pass. HELUT then parsed the generated JSON and compiled a graph with five inputs, three lookup tables, no flip-flops, and one output in 0.0032 seconds. The filmed rerun later reports its own compile observation.
scenes.headline: Five inputs. Three lookup tables.
scenes.subhead: Yosys + ABC · tables up to four inputs

scenes.voiceover: Five input bits have exactly 32 possible patterns, small enough to test without sampling. The clear-equivalence command enumerated every one. For each row it evaluated the ordinary netlist simulator and the noise-free multilinear graph, then compared the output bit. 32 rows entered. 32 matched. Result: pass. This establishes that lowering the synthesized tables into HELUT preserved the majority function over its entire input space. It does not establish encryption yet. Keeping that receipt separate matters, because the next pass proves a different thing.
scenes.headline: All thirty-two vote patterns
scenes.subhead: Clear simulator ≡ trivial multilinear graph
scenes.kicker: Step three · prove the plain shape

scenes.voiceover: Now the encrypted path in the initial receipt. SING means stimuli in, golden out: run each stimulus through the encrypted evaluator, decrypt the chosen output inside the harness, and compare it with the clear result. At polynomial size N=16, the harness again covered all 32 vote patterns. Every decrypted decision matched. The complete run took 0.0089 seconds, or 0.28 milliseconds per row. But this is a correctness demonstration, not production security. Its own receipt prints 8 modeled classical bits, and the bootstrap key uses an exact-noiseless construction. Fast, exhaustive, and intentionally insecure are all true at once.
scenes.headline: Thirty-two encrypted rows. Thirty-two matches.
scenes.subhead: Initial run · N=16 demonstration · 0.0089 seconds total

scenes.voiceover: Finally, the initial receipt runs the same three-table netlist at polynomial size N=1024 on Metal. This run covered two deterministic endpoint stimuli, not all 32: the production-size receipt is bounded to two rows. Both matched the golden model. Total wall time was 2.7189 seconds, or about 1.36 seconds per row. The hardness line reports 175.7 modeled classical bits. Modeled is essential. And the receipt still says exact-noiseless construction, so this is a production-parameter-size execution receipt, not a noisy bootstrap-key robustness proof or a blanket security audit.
scenes.headline: Production parameter size. Two rows.
scenes.subhead: Initial run · N=1024 · PASS · 2.7189 seconds

scenes.voiceover: One more receipt belongs beside the authored panels: the literal terminal rerun filmed after the script was drafted. This is a real Bash pseudo-terminal at normal speed. It types the complete Verilog, verifies a byte-for-byte match with the tracked source, synthesizes three lookup tables, checks both endpoints, exhausts all 32 clear rows, exhausts all 32 encrypted rows at N=16, and runs two deterministic rows at N=1024 on Metal. The values differ slightly from the first receipt. The initial run recorded 0.0089 seconds and 2.7189 seconds. This filmed rerun recorded 0.0095 seconds and 2.5320 seconds. Both runs passed. They are two observations, not a timing distribution or evidence of stable performance. The footage proves that these commands executed; the static panels remain the readable scientific receipts.
scenes.label: Filmed rerun · 2026-09-04 · normal speed

scenes.voiceover: Put the layers beside one another and the result is useful without being inflated. Yosys mapped a five-input majority function into three lookup tables. The clear path matched all 32 inputs. The encrypted demonstration path matched all 32 again. The production-parameter-size Metal path matched two endpoint rows. The later filmed rerun repeated those outcomes, with separate timing observations. Outside those receipts are the stronger claims: no multiparty voting protocol, no proof that the host learns nothing from timing or metadata, no noisy-key result, and no exhaustive sweep at N=1024. The circuit works in the harness. The surrounding election system has not been built, and the episode will not pretend otherwise.
scenes.headline: What the receipts prove
bullets: Yosys: 5 inputs → 3 mapped tables → 1 output
Clear path: 32 of 32 patterns match in both runs
Encrypted N=16 path: 32 of 32 match in both runs
Metal N=1024 path: 2 of 2 endpoints match in both runs

scenes.voiceover: One more thing, because scale is the honest test of a compiler. Everything so far used three lookup tables. The same path also takes a real processor: a RISC-V core synthesized to 4,785 lookup tables and 1,565 flip-flops. That matters because flip-flops mean state. The circuit has to be clocked, and every encrypted register has to survive every tick. The program is deliberately tiny: put one in a register, store it to memory, read it back. If encrypted state were broken, that sequence would fail immediately. Here is the boundary, though. The host implements the memory, so it sees instruction addresses and data. Only the processor itself is evaluated encrypted.
scenes.headline: Three lookup tables, then a processor
scenes.subhead: 4785 lookup tables · 1565 flip-flops · encrypted state
scenes.kicker: Coda · the same path, much bigger

scenes.voiceover: Same compiler, same encrypted evaluator, a very different circuit. The capture compiles both designs live: the majority circuit is five inputs, three lookup tables, no state. The processor is 102 inputs, 4,785 lookup tables, and 1,565 flip-flops. Then it runs that tiny program under encryption for 48 ticks. Watch the program counter advance by four each fetch. At tick 16 the store writes one to address zero. At tick 25 the host serves that same one back. 48 of 48 ticks matched the clear model, including every flip-flop, in 2.4828 seconds. And the honest part: this ran on CPU, at 4.0 modeled classical bits, and the host is the memory.
scenes.label: Coda · encrypted RISC-V · normal speed

scenes.voiceover: The worthwhile part is not that majority is a difficult function. It is that the privacy boundary is understandable, the input space is small enough to exhaust, and the production-size claim can be separated cleanly from the demonstration. The source, generated netlist, six full logs, curated receipt, two literal captures with their own manifests and transcripts, commands, dates, and hashes are all preserved. On a matching toolchain, there is a path back from the sentence to the run. Five encrypted bits entered this harness. One decision bit was revealed. A three-table vote and a whole processor came out of the same compiler. Everything stronger remains outside the receipt. That is how a small experiment earns an episode.
scenes.headline: The path back is the point
scenes.subhead: Source. Netlist. Six logs. One bounded result.

prerequisites: Yosys 0.68+ with ABC for the synthesis and endpoint stages
Apple silicon with Metal for the N=1024 stage

yosys -Q -p 'read_verilog Hardware/RTL/Examples/private_majority5.v; prep -top private_majority5; eval -set votes 0 -show proposal_passes; eval -set votes 31 -show proposal_passes'

captures.timingNote: These are two individual observations, not a timing distribution or stability benchmark.

This is not a deployed multiparty voting protocol and does not prove host privacy.
N=16 is a demonstration parameter with 8.0 modeled classical bits.
The N=1024 run checks two deterministic rows, not all 32 rows.
The 175.7-bit figure is modeled, not independently audited.

prerequisites: no Yosys or Metal device required; both netlists are checked in and the run is CPU-only

captures.timingNote: Three individual observations on one machine. This is not a timing distribution, a stability claim, or a performance benchmark.

The host implements memory. It drives mem_ready/mem_rdata and observes mem_valid/mem_addr/mem_wstrb/mem_wdata, so instruction addresses and memory data are visible to the host and appear in the trace in the clear.
The SING harness owns the key and decrypts outputs in-process to compare them with a clear golden model.
The encrypted evaluation covers the synthesized picorv32 netlist, not the host ROM or host RAM.
This run used CPU blind rotation. The Metal path was skipped by --cpu-only.

The program is three meaningful instructions in a tiny ROM padded with unbounded no-ops, not a general workload, not an operating system, and not a production encrypted CPU.

The lookup-table comparison against the majority circuit is a scale contrast, not a normalized area metric: the majority netlist was mapped up to four-input tables while this PicoRV32 netlist tops out at three-input tables.

episodes.title: One Callsign, Three Acts
episodes.youtubeTitle: GNU Radio Recovered a Demo Callsign — Then a Yosys Circuit Matched It
episodes.description: A literal, reproducible closed-loop experiment sends CQ CQ CQ DE AB0CDE AB0CDE K through locally generated BPSK-like IQ and a simulated GNU Radio channel at noise_voltage=0.0. All 27 bytes return exactly; a fixed six-byte, 48-input, 47-LUT Yosys circuit reports callsign completions at payload bytes 17 and 24. A clear scalar host loop then produces 908 expected and observed hits across 10,000 evaluations of 22 unique windows. Finally, one AB0CDE window runs on the N=8 encrypted demonstration path, with engine and key setup excluded from its timer. No antenna, OTA signal, interception, general regex engine, native tensor batch, encrypted stream, or production-security claim is involved. The literal terminal capture, full raw log, hashes, and reproduction commands are preserved. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: This episode begins with a demonstration callsign and ends with a receipt. I built a circuit that recognizes exactly six ASCII bytes: AB0CDE. Then I gave the same circuit three deliberately different jobs. First, match callsigns recovered from a local GNU Radio loop through the clear Boolean oracle. Second, repeat recovered windows through that same clear path. Third, freeze one callsign and evaluate that one window on the encrypted demonstration path. Those are three acts, not one blended claim. The signal is local, the footage is literal, and every boundary stays on screen.
scenes.headline: One callsign. Three acts.
scenes.subhead: Local IQ. Recovered bytes. A circuit says yes.

scenes.voiceover: Here is the channel before any circuit sees a byte. GNU Radio starts from a finite vector in memory. It maps bits to plus or minus one, repeats each symbol four times, creates complex baseband samples, passes them through the channel-model block, hard-slices the result, and finds an 0xAA55 preamble to recover byte alignment. The transmitted payload is CQ CQ CQ DE AB0CDE AB0CDE K. For the filmed receipt, noise voltage is 0.0. 27 bytes went in and the same 27 came back, with zero byte differences. This is a deterministic local loop. There was no antenna, no over-the-air signal, and nothing was intercepted.
scenes.headline: A radio chain with no radio link
scenes.subhead: CQ CQ CQ DE AB0CDE AB0CDE K · 27 bytes out, 27 bytes back

scenes.voiceover: The detector is intentionally concrete. Six eight-bit ports are compared with the ASCII values for A, B, zero, C, D, and E. That makes 48 input bits and one match output. Yosys and ABC lower the authored Verilog into 47 two-input lookup-table cells, and the Yosys check pass reports zero problems. HELUT does not receive a string search function. It receives that generated lookup-table graph. The rolling helper learns its six-byte window from ports named char zero through char five, packs each byte least-significant bit first, and ticks the netlist. This is an exact, case-sensitive, fixed-literal circuit. Calling it a general regular-expression engine would claim something we did not build.
scenes.headline: Six bytes become forty-eight wires
scenes.subhead: Exact ASCII literal · 47 two-input lookup tables · one match bit

scenes.voiceover: After GNU Radio stops, Python feeds the recovered payload to HELUT one byte at a time. The first five bytes only warm the six-byte window. A match appears when the final E arrives. In this payload, the first callsign occupies zero-based byte positions 12 through 17. The second occupies 19 through 24. So the expected completion positions are 17 and 24. The clear netlist oracle reports exactly that list. The runner also scans the recovered bytes in software and compares against the callsign positions in the transmitted payload. Both comparisons must agree or the command exits with failure. In the filmed run, the recovered bytes were exact and both callsign windows survived.
scenes.headline: Both callsigns land exactly
scenes.subhead: Match completion indices: [17, 24]
scenes.kicker: Act I · recovered stream · clear oracle

scenes.voiceover: Act two asks a different question: can the host-to-library hinge repeat the clear circuit many times and keep the answer straight? A 27-byte payload contains 22 overlapping six-byte windows. The runner cycles those windows in order until it has made 10,000 scalar calls. 10,000 is 454 complete cycles of 22, plus 12 extra windows. Each complete cycle contains the two callsigns, and those first 12 remainder windows contain neither. 454 times 2 gives 908 expected hits. HELUT reports 908. The filmed wall observation is 113.34 milliseconds. But this is not batch acceleration. It is a clear scalar host loop, not a native tensor batch and not encrypted throughput.
scenes.headline: Ten thousand calls, one at a time
scenes.subhead: 22 unique windows · 908 expected · 908 observed

scenes.voiceover: Only act three enters the encrypted demonstration mode. The runner selects the first recovered AB0CDE window, opens the fixed-seed N=8 engine, and then starts the stopwatch around the six feed calls. Five calls warm the window; the sixth evaluates the circuit. The decrypted demonstration result is one, matching the expected bit. The filmed evaluation observation is 1.1 milliseconds, but engine and key setup happened before that timer. N=8 is a tiny demonstration parameter, not production security. One frozen window is not an encrypted radio stream. The honest result is narrower and still useful: this generated 47-table circuit returns the right bit on one encrypted demonstration input.
scenes.headline: Encrypt one callsign, not the stream
scenes.subhead: AB0CDE · N=8 demonstration · result 1

scenes.voiceover: This is the literal run, not a reconstruction. First, the authored Verilog and its hash. Next, Yosys reloads the generated netlist: 48 input bits, 47 lookup tables, one output, and zero check problems. Then GNU Radio creates the local IQ stream and recovers all 27 bytes. HELUT reports the callsign at completion positions 17 and 24. The final screen separates the other acts: 10,000 clear scalar windows, 908 expected and observed hits; then one AB0CDE window on the N=8 encrypted demonstration path. The tape ends with the no-antenna verdict and hashes of the source, netlist, runner, and full raw log.
scenes.label: Literal run · 2026-09-04 · normal speed

scenes.voiceover: The durable receipt now fits in four rows. Radio first: 27 transmitted bytes, 27 recovered bytes, zero differences, and callsign completions at 17 and 24. Circuit next: six exact bytes become 48 input bits, 47 two-input lookup tables, and one result bit. Repetition next: 10,000 clear scalar window evaluations, built from 22 unique windows, produce 908 expected and observed hits. Encryption last: one recovered AB0CDE window enters the N=8 demonstration path and returns one. The tape, MP4, authored source, canonical netlist, runner, transcript, manifest, and complete unfiltered log all have hashes. The raw log is preserved beside the capture rather than existing only under an ignored build directory.
scenes.headline: The receipt in four rows
bullets: 27 / 27 bytes exact · callsign completions [17, 24]
6 bytes · 48 input bits · 47 LUT2 cells · 1 output
10,000 clear scalar windows · 22 unique · 908 / 908
1 AB0CDE window · encrypted-demo N=8 · result 1

scenes.voiceover: Now draw the box around the result. The source was a local vector and no antenna was used, so this is not reception or interception. The channel-model block was present, but noise voltage was zero for deterministic footage, so the run does not establish tolerance to noise. The circuit recognizes one fixed literal, so it is not a general regex engine. Acts one and two use the clear Boolean oracle. 10,000 means scalar calls over 22 repeating source windows, not a native tensor batch and not encrypted throughput. Act three encrypts one window at N=8; it is not an encrypted stream, and N=8 is not a production security parameter. Finally, every timing number is one local observation. The receipts prove execution and agreement, not a performance distribution.
scenes.headline: What this run is not
bullets: Not OTA reception or interception
Not a channel-noise tolerance result
Not a general regex engine
Not native tensor batching or encrypted throughput
Not an encrypted stream or production security

scenes.voiceover: That separation is the point. GNU Radio recovered a recognizable payload through a local baseband loop. A generated lookup-table circuit found both copies of the callsign on the clear path. The same clear circuit survived 10,000 scalar invocations with the exact expected count. Then one recovered window crossed the encrypted demonstration path and returned the right bit. None of those facts needs an antenna story, a batch-performance story, or a production-security story to be interesting. The source, netlist, literal footage, full output, commands, and hashes are preserved. AB0CDE went through the machine, and the path back to every sentence is still there.

episodes.title: The Skeptic's Benchmark
episodes.youtubeTitle: Does Tensorized Verilog Actually Help? An Honest HELUT Benchmark
episodes.description: A technically informed skeptic asks the right questions: what problem does tensorizing a synthesized circuit solve, is it more efficient than native HDL execution, and why target Apple silicon? This episode answers with a sealed matched-circuit receipt rather than a selected timing. On one 8-bit ripple adder, the historical warmed-graph comparison shows graph amortization against scalar Verilator, but the accepted paired scope counts deterministic preparation, synchronized execution, strict readback, and the same ordered digest on both sides. At B=65,536 HELUT measured 8.544 milliseconds versus 7.422 milliseconds for 16-worker Verilator: HELUT remained 15.1 percent slower, with no paired crossover through that width. The digest is required shared work inside both timers and is not subtracted to synthesize a separate evaluator ratio. A separate HELUT graph sweep reaches 1,048,576 lanes, but high-width native values are projections on another fixture, not same-width paired results. The episode also preserves the lane-distinct correctness gate: 65,536 distinct assignments, 589,824 checked output bits, zero mismatches, and a corruption control that moves the digest. A 688-LUT, 26-DFF Enigma M3 netlist separately runs through HELUT's trivial, noise-free N=1024 Metal path and agrees with the clear oracle on a 25-letter transcript. Apple silicon matters here because host orchestration, Metal shaders, and MPSGraph share one physical memory pool; that is an architectural rationale, not a measured win over a discrete GPU. No encryption, sequential-lane throughput, general HDL superiority, CXXRTL result, Apple exclusivity, or cross-platform conclusion is claimed. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: Episode zero answers what HELUT is and where it loses. This episode is the receipt underneath that answer: how the comparison was built, what it cost to make it fair, and every correction I had to publish along the way. If you want the number without the method, you already have it. HELUT is 15.1 percent slower than 16-worker Verilator on matched work. What follows is why I trust that figure more than the flattering one I started with.
scenes.headline: Does tensorized Verilog actually help?
scenes.subhead: The method behind the number, not the pitch.

scenes.voiceover: Same circuit lineage on both sides. Same deterministic stimulus. Every digest matches, or the timings are void. Read the two scopes separately. BASELINE is the historical flattering row: HELUT's warmed synchronized graph call against a scalar native loop that also assigns, evaluates, reads, and hashes. It demonstrates sampled graph amortization, not end-to-end throughput. PAIRED is the accepted verdict: deterministic preparation, all input writes, synchronized execution, strict output readback, and the ordered digest counted on both sides, with Verilator using 16 persistent workers. At 65,536 lanes HELUT is 8.544 milliseconds and native is 7.422. HELUT remains 15.1 percent slower, and there is no paired crossover through the largest tested width. The next screen is correctness rather than speed: 65,536 different assignments and 589,824 output bits checked against their own oracles, with zero mismatches. Last, the teeth: corrupt lane 37 of 256 and the digest changes and the checker reports five mismatches. A gate that cannot fail is decoration.
scenes.label: SEALED RECEIPT PLAYBACK · final source and receipt hashes shown · no timing rerun

scenes.voiceover: First, what is actually in the comparison. HELUT is not a replacement for an event-driven simulator. Yosys does the front end and synthesis, ABC packs the gates into lookup tables, and HELUT starts from that two-state netlist of tables, flip-flops and ports. It has no model of behavioural Verilog, propagation delay, signal strength, or the X and Z values a real simulator tracks. So bit accuracy is not the selling point; Verilator and Icarus already own that. What the tensor form adds is two axes. B is how many independent copies of the circuit ride along together. N is how many coefficients stand in for one logical wire, where N equals one is plain Boolean and N equals 1,024 matches the polynomial size the encrypted side uses. Those axes expose parallel work. Whether the machine executes that work faster than a compiler does is the measurement, not the definition.
scenes.headline: A two-state netlist, not a Verilog simulator
scenes.subhead: Yosys and ABC do the front end · B batches instances · N is wire degree

scenes.voiceover: Same experiment, running now, not replayed. A synthesized Enigma rotor machine: 688 lookup tables, 26 flip-flops, 10 inputs, 8 outputs, evaluated as tensors at polynomial size 1024. Read the labels first, because the tool volunteers its own limits. Batch mode: legacy broadcast. Encoding: constant-fill, trivial, noise-free. That is not encrypted data and nothing pretends otherwise. Compile lands under 40 milliseconds. The first tick costs about 0.3 seconds because it pays to build and specialize the Metal kernels, and the 9 ticks after it average roughly 15 milliseconds. Then the gate that matters. A clear oracle written in Swift, which never touches the GPU, and the Metal path both produce the same 25 letters: KEINEBESONDERENEREIGNISSE. Result, PASS. Second screen, three more runs back to back: 66.5, 67.1, and 67.2 ticks per second. The run before them read 68.5. That spread across four passes in one sitting is why a single number here would be fiction.
scenes.label: LIVE RUN · recorded 2026-09-05 · not a replay

scenes.voiceover: Now the caveat that used to undercut the most quotable number here, and the receipt that closed it. The old clock benchmark filled every batch lane with the same encoded value. Output tensors were written, but the timed loop never read them back and never hashed them per lane. That scaling table measured graph shape, allocation, and memory pressure, not useful work, and calling it a thousand-way verified simulation would have been a lie. Three things had to change before any batching claim was allowed: every lane doing independent work, a canonical checksum over ordered outputs, and a deliberately corrupted bit that makes the checksum fail. All three exist now. At B=65,536 the distinct-lane path carries 65,536 different input assignments, checks all 589,824 output bits against per-lane clear oracles, and reports 0 mismatches under one digest, with 511 distinct output signatures. And it has teeth: corrupting one lane moves the digest and surfaces the mismatch. That is verified batching, not proof of superior throughput.
scenes.headline: The existing batch sweep repeats one feed
scenes.subhead: B=1000 is not yet 1000 independently checked vectors
scenes.kicker: The number that cannot be oversold

scenes.voiceover: For most of this project's life nobody had measured the native comparison. Now there is a Verilator baseline over the same emitted circuit lineage, the same deterministic assignments, and the same digest gate. The historical rows preserve the old scope: one warmed synchronized HELUT graph call versus a scalar Verilator loop that assigns, evaluates, reads, and hashes. Those rows can show a sampled HELUT win at large B, but the comparison is intentionally asymmetric and the sampled threshold moves between runs. The paired row is the result to hand a skeptic. It counts deterministic assignment and input packing, synchronized execution, strict readback and materialization, and the ordered digest on both sides, with native using 16 persistent workers. At B=65,536 HELUT measured 8.544 milliseconds versus native at 7.422. That is 1.151 times native, or 15.1 percent slower. No paired crossover was observed through B=65,536.
scenes.headline: Is it faster than native HDL?
scenes.subhead: Historical graph amortizes · paired scope remains 15.1% short
scenes.kicker: The Reddit question, answered both ways

scenes.voiceover: The useful result is not just the final ratio; it is the recovery path. The original decomposed HELUT paired median at 65,536 lanes was 32.414 milliseconds. Flat lane-major output storage removed tens of thousands of tiny allocations. Precomputed port metadata and exact pointer decoding repaired assignment, packing, and readback overhead. A cost-selected constant-fill Shannon graph reduced the live logical arithmetic in this fixture from 1,116 operations to 194. Finally, an exact degree-one input pack kept every one of the 1,114,112 writes but cut the packing median from 1.240 milliseconds to 0.529. The final HELUT median is 8.544 milliseconds. Its phase medians are 0.030 for assignment, 0.529 for packing, 0.766 for graph execution, 0.548 for strict decode, and 6.677 for the ordered digest. Native is still ahead by 1.122 milliseconds. No one non-digest micro-phase is large enough to close that gap alone, so the next work is a combination, not a relabeled timer. One more thing the table says out loud: the paired ratio narrows at every width tested, from 77 times native at a single lane to 1.151 at 65,536, with no reversal. That is eight steps in one direction. It is also where the fixture ends, because 65,536 is the entire input space of a 16-bit adder, so a wider test needs a bigger circuit rather than a bigger batch.
scenes.headline: We recovered the host path; native still leads
scenes.subhead: 32.414 ms → 8.544 ms HELUT · 1.122 ms paired gap remains
scenes.kicker: Profile first · preserve every failed claim

scenes.voiceover: A previous draft tried to turn the shared digest into a separate evaluator headline. That was not defensible. Both backends hash the same lane, wire, and value words in the same order: 12 bytes per output bit, about 7.1 million bytes at 65,536 lanes. The accepted paired contract includes that work inside both timers. It is real output consumption and a correctness gate, not a tax we may remove after seeing the result. Native's narrower prepared timer excludes assignment and digest while including worker synchronization, evaluation, and output collection. HELUT's graph timer is a different boundary. Subtracting independent medians or comparing those unequal phases does not produce an honest native-evaluation ratio. The claim is therefore the direct paired result: 15.1 percent behind, digest included, no crossover through the tested range.
scenes.headline: Shared work stays in the contract
scenes.subhead: Digest inside both timers · no post-hoc subtraction

scenes.voiceover: The accepted comparison was frozen before its one retained run. One emitted Verilog circuit feeds both lineages. The lane corpus is deterministic and exhaustive at 65,536. HELUT rewrites every input buffer, executes one synchronized graph, strictly reads and materializes every output, and computes the canonical ordered digest. Native prepares every assignment, evaluates and stores every output with a persistent 16-worker pool, and computes the same digest. All of that stays inside the paired boundary. Five timed passes are retained at each of eight widths, and every raw array remains visible. This fills one bounded row: one combinational 8-bit ripple adder on one Mac. Still open are a sequential design with independent state per lane, an authored-RTL baseline beside the artifact-matched one, CXXRTL, other hosts, and a constant-total-work sweep. Naming the open rows is part of the result.
scenes.headline: Same circuit. Same work. Same digest.
scenes.subhead: One combinational result · sequential and broader baselines still open
scenes.kicker: The contract was written first · one row is filled

scenes.voiceover: Enigma makes that pattern concrete. Host code organizes rotor, ring, and starting-position settings, plugboard pairs, and candidate populations. Wide Metal kernels sweep many settings or scoring lanes at once. The host then filters survivors, tightens constraints, breeds the next generation, and starts another round. With shared buffers those phases can live in one memory pool instead of paying a staging tax at every boundary. Large candidate tensors can spend real unified memory. But capacity is not throughput, and the repository has a receipt that proves it. At N=1024 and B=1000, resident memory peaked near 6 gigabytes and the tick rate fell to 13.62 per second, against roughly 69 at B=1. So the defensible claim is that unified memory opens this design space. Beating a discrete GPU inside it is a separate measurement nobody here has taken.
scenes.headline: Build candidates on the CPU; sweep them on the GPU
scenes.subhead: Settings · tables · ciphertext · scores · survivors · repeat
scenes.kicker: Why Enigma makes the architecture visible

scenes.voiceover: So what does HELUT actually solve today? It bridges supported Yosys lookup-table graphs into a Metal tensor substrate, and that substrate agrees with independent clear checks bit for bit on the bounded receipts. The batch axis is verified rather than broadcast: 65,536 assignments, 589,824 output bits, zero mismatches, and a digest that moves under deliberate corruption. On performance, the historical warmed graph can amortize against a scalar native loop, but that is not the paired verdict. Under the accepted end-to-end boundary HELUT is 15.1 percent slower than 16-worker Verilator at 65,536 lanes, with no paired crossover through that width. The shared digest stays inside both timers, and no 12-fold evaluator result is synthesized from unequal phase boundaries. A separate HELUT graph sweep reaches a million lanes, but its high-width native line is projected on another fixture. Cleartext paired superiority remains unproved. The tensor path remains valuable for shared encrypted machinery and searchable truth tables, where the next episodes put different claims under different gates.
scenes.headline: The current verdict

Proved: 589,824 lane-distinct output bits, 0 mismatches

Not claimed: encrypted speed, sequential lanes, Apple exclusivity

scenes.voiceover: The tensor path gets more interesting when the circuit is not merely executed. A lookup table can be lifted out of zeros and ones into continuous values, searched against a target, and pushed back toward discrete hardware. That is melt and freeze, and it arrives with its own bill. Did the frozen circuit stay correct? Did the topology change? Did the resource count improve? Will Yosys take the emitted result back? And what happens when the search refuses to go binary? Episode 15 puts the passing two-bit control, the round-trip checker, its negative control, and the failed M4 run on the same screen. It also answers the last question a skeptic asked me: how this compares with logic simplification that already exists. The combined search-and-map flow has been measured against an identical ABC recipe, and it came back a tie on every run.
scenes.headline: If not better simulation, then what?
scenes.subhead: Next: melt the truth tables, freeze them again, and inspect the proof.

episodes.title: Melt. Freeze. Prove.
episodes.youtubeTitle: Melt and Freeze a Hardware Circuit — What HELUT Actually Proves
episodes.description: HELUT's melt/freeze path is shown as implemented, and the join it used to be missing is now closed. Fixed-topology LUT truth tables are lifted from binary entries to Float32 values, selected LUTs are searched with evolutionary mutation and crossover, and a threshold returns the mutable region to discrete tables when target fitness is preserved. The searched result is then emitted, re-synthesized by Yosys, and proven equivalent to a behavioural Verilog reference by SAT (miter -equiv + minisat over the post-abc -lut 6 artifact); corrupting one discovered entry yields a counterexample. The cold open is a live run: on an 8-bit adder with 16 LUTs, a 2-LUT melt trained on 64 of 65,536 rows (0.10%) is formally proven over all 65,536 assignments, and the erased baseline is REFUTED on every row. A low-budget failure control is shown too: melting 8 of 8 LUTs at 120 generations returns a fully binary, zero-fractional, still-incorrect circuit at fitness -16; the same fixture proves at 500 generations, so this is budget sensitivity rather than a hard method frontier. Sequential repair is also shown live: a transition behind one DFF is erased, rediscovered as q_next = q XOR x, and proven by post-ABC equiv_induct over every matched Boolean state and all enable/reset/input combinations, with a reset-to-divergence counterexample when one discovered INIT bit is flipped. Open: arbitrary topology, convergence guarantees, coupled or multi-DFF repair, and any area or depth win over Yosys/ABC (6 LUTs vs 6). An archived M4 targeted-melt failure remains visible. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: Watch the rows column. That is an 8-bit adder: 16 lookup tables and 65,536 possible inputs. Two tables are erased. The repair search sees only 64 rows: 0.10 percent. It finds the missing logic, then Yosys re-synthesizes the result and SAT proves equivalence to behavioural addition across all 65,536 assignments. The erased baseline is REFUTED, so the circuit was genuinely broken. On this fixture, search did not enumerate the domain and the independent proof covers unseen rows. One fixture is not an asymptotic complexity result. Second screen, the failure control. Erase 2 of 8 tables and it proves. 4, it proves. 6, it proves. Erase all 8 at this 120-generation budget and it returns fully binary but wrong, fitness -16. That is not where the method stops: the same fixture proves at 500 generations in episode 3's live gate. Binarity is not correctness, and search budget matters.
scenes.label: LIVE RUN · recorded 2026-09-05 · prebuilt test bundle · not a replay

scenes.voiceover: The search never saw 65,472 of those input rows, and the proof covers them anyway. That is the result worth sitting with, so here is the machinery behind it. A lookup table in HELUT holds truth-table entries that are normally exact zeros and ones. Melting lets selected entries become floating-point values in between, so a search can move them. Freezing pushes them back to exact binary. Proving means handing the resulting discrete circuit to a tool that had no part in the search and letting it try to break the result. This episode shows the controlled pass, the checker that catches corruption, a low-budget failure control, and the exact sentence where a general claim would outrun the evidence.
scenes.headline: Melt. Freeze. Prove.
scenes.subhead: Continuous truth tables are useful only if the discrete circuit survives.

scenes.voiceover: What melts is the INIT table inside a lookup-table block. INIT is the Verilog parameter that spells out a table's truth values, and TensorLUT pads every supported table to 64 Float32 entries, six inputs being the widest cell it accepts. Evaluation uses the multilinear extension: each of the 64 entries is weighted by how strongly the inputs point at its corner of the cube. Feed it exact zeros and ones and only one weight is nonzero, so it returns the same entry Boolean logic would. Feed it fractions and it interpolates between corners. A freeze mask then picks which whole blocks mutation may touch. Wires, connections, lookup-table count, and flip-flop count never move, because the genome is nothing but INIT floats. No operator exists that could move them. That matters, because a phrase like genetic hardware implies topology search. This is narrower: evolutionary search over truth-table parameters on a fixed graph. Useful for inverse design or targeted repair. Not structural logic synthesis.
scenes.headline: Topology stays fixed; INIT values move
scenes.subhead: 64 Float32 entries per LUT6 · frozen or mutable by block

scenes.voiceover: The strongest controlled example is deliberately tiny. A two-bit adder built from four lookup tables, scheduled in two execution levels, meaning two rounds of evaluation where everything inside a round can be computed at once. Four primary input bits, three output bits, so the entire combinational domain is 16 assignments. The first level computes the low sum with XOR and the low carry with AND. The second level combines the two upper input bits with that carry. Because every possible input fits on one page, comparing all 16 rows later is exhaustive for this function rather than a sample. Small does not mean weak evidence here. It means the word proof can be used literally.
scenes.headline: A four-LUT two-bit adder
scenes.subhead: 4 inputs · 3 outputs · 16 complete rows · 2 logic levels
scenes.kicker: The microscope · small enough to exhaust

scenes.voiceover: The targeted experiment freezes the two low-bit tables and lets only the two carry-stage tables move. 64 entries each, so the mutable region is 128 floats, and every one of them is wiped to 0.5: maximally undecided under this representation. The frozen blocks keep their original binary tables byte for byte, and that is the first falsifiable gate. If mutation or crossover disturbs a single frozen entry, the test fails. It is worth being precise about what is being asked here. The carry-stage tables were declared as all zeros to begin with, so there is no correct answer hiding underneath the wipe. The search has to discover the carry logic, not remember it, while the rest of the circuit stays fixed.
scenes.headline: Two LUTs frozen, two LUTs melted
scenes.subhead: 128 mutable floats wiped to 0.5 · 128 frozen floats preserved
scenes.kicker: Freeze what is known · erase what is not

scenes.voiceover: The implemented search is evolutionary, not gradient descent. 48 chromosomes, each one a full copy of the lookup-table entries. Sparse Gaussian mutation nudges mutable values, occasional jumps land exactly on zero or one, and crossover swaps whole 64-entry blocks between parents. The objective has two terms. The first is what the code calls crypto fitness: the negative sum of squared output error, so zero is perfect and everything else is worse. The second is a binarity penalty, the sum of w times one minus w over every mutable entry, which is zero at zero and at one and largest at one half. Its lambda weight sits at nothing for the first tenth of the run and then ramps up, so the search fits the target first and feels pressure toward binary tables later. The two-bit control pins all of it: 120 generations, seed 0x7A6E17, a lambda ceiling of 12, and one binary polish attempt at the end.
scenes.headline: Mutation, crossover, target error, binarity pressure
scenes.subhead: Population 48 · 120 generations · fixed seed 0x7A6E17

scenes.voiceover: Polish proposes a discrete chromosome by thresholding each mutable entry at 0.5. Below becomes zero, at or above becomes one. HELUT then re-scores that hard version against the same target and accepts it only if hard crypto fitness comes out no more than 0.001 worse than the soft version it would replace. That is a real safety gate, and it deserves an accurate name. It is a check against this experiment's target, not a theorem about equivalence. Zero fractional entries tells you the result is discrete. On its own it tells you nothing about whether the result is right.
scenes.headline: Snap at 0.5, then score again
scenes.subhead: Accept only if hard target fitness stays within 0.001
scenes.kicker: Thresholding is a proposal, not a proof

scenes.voiceover: Two gates, both live. First the freeze mask: 6 tests, zero failures, and the one that matters is the targeted melt, which discovers the carry logic while the known tables stay byte-identical. If mutation touched a single frozen entry that test fails. Second gate, the hardware round trip. The circuit is emitted as Verilog, handed to Yosys, mapped by ABC, reloaded, and compared: 48 output bits over all 16 inputs. Every claim here has a matching negative control, because a gate that cannot fail is decoration. Corrupt one table, 4 mismatches. Corrupt a discovered entry, 3 of 48. Now read the two SEQUENTIAL lines, because those are new. A state transition behind a flip-flop was erased, rediscovered as q-next equals q XOR x, and proven by induction over every matched state and every enable and reset combination. Flip one discovered bit and induction refuses, handing back a reset-to-divergence trace. That is repair with state.
scenes.label: LIVE RUN · recorded 2026-09-05 · prebuilt test bundle · not a replay

scenes.voiceover: An older identity-round-trip test closes the emitter and checker loop. It takes the unmutated four-table adder, emits it as six-input LUT Verilog, hands the file to Yosys, maps it with ABC, writes a fresh JSON netlist, reloads that netlist, and compares three outputs across all 16 inputs. 48 output bits agree. Flip one INIT entry and today's run reports 4 mismatches; the assertion only requires at least one, so four is observed rather than pinned. This older receipt did not join search to proof. The newer searched-elite test now does: search the erased tables, emit the discovered result, re-synthesize it, prove the full domain, then flip one discovered entry and demand a counterexample.
scenes.headline: Emit → Yosys → reload → exhaust all rows
scenes.subhead: 48 output bits agree · corrupted INIT observed: 4 mismatches

scenes.voiceover: The archived M4 run is the counterweight, and it used a different configuration from the two-bit control: population 16, lambda ceiling 10, 150 generations of exploring followed by 250 of squeezing. Exploring means chasing target fitness with the binarity penalty switched off. Squeezing means turning that penalty up to force the entries binary. The graph held 925 lookup tables and 49 flip-flops, 16 tables mutable and 909 frozen. Exploring worked: sampled fitness climbed from -4.25 to -1.9. Squeezing did not. It finished with 118 entries still non-binary and target fitness back down at -4.94. A Verilog file came out anyway, because the emitter thresholds whatever it is handed. No equivalence check ever said that file was correct, so this is a failure, not a near-success parked behind an artifact path. The project's answer was to stop searching for plugboard reciprocity in truth-table entries and enforce it structurally instead.
scenes.headline: A larger targeted melt did not freeze
scenes.subhead: 925 LUT · 49 DFF · 16 mutable · 118 entries still fractional
scenes.kicker: The failure stays in the ledger

scenes.voiceover: So how does this compare with logic simplification as it already exists? Yosys and ABC rewrite Boolean structure. They remove redundancy, merge cells, map to a target library, and trade depth against area. The HELUT search holds structure still and changes lookup-table values to fit a target while pushing them toward binary. Its objective carries no area term, no depth term, and no timing or power term. So the two are not doing the same job. The fair question is what happens when you run the combined flow: discover a new discrete function on fixed topology, emit it, then let ABC strip whatever redundancy that creates, and hand both the original and the discovered circuit to the same mapper. That flow has now run end to end on six circuits. The next screen is its receipt, and it is not the answer a promoter would want.
scenes.headline: HELUT and ABC optimize different things
scenes.subhead: Different knob, and the combined flow has now been measured

scenes.voiceover: One flow, printed at the top, runs identically on both sides: read the LUT6 model, flatten, optimize, techmap, then abc -lut 6, then check. Area is the mapped lookup-table count. Depth is the worst output cone. Proof is a miter and a SAT solve against independent behavioural Verilog. Before mapping, the search does real work. The 8-bit adder falls from 41 tables to 16. The multiplexer halves. The multiplier drops from 18 to 6. If I stopped the screen there, I could sell you a simplifier. Then the same recipe maps both sides, and the columns land on top of each other. 14 against 14. Three against three. Six against six. Across six circuits and three seeds, that is 18 results: zero wins, 18 ties, zero losses on count, and the same on depth. Every retained finalist was proved. The receipt calls it an honest null, because the search removed redundant cones and ABC removed the same redundancy. The boundary line is on screen too: these are mapping proxies, not area, delay, frequency, or power.
scenes.label: PRESERVED RECEIPT · identical abc -lut 6 on both sides · measured null

scenes.voiceover: Four rows, then. One: a Yosys lookup-table graph can be lifted into continuous truth-table parameters and evaluated on Metal. Two: a freeze mask protects known tables while a deterministic evolutionary search discovers an acceptable discrete solution. Three: TensorLUT Verilog survives Yosys re-synthesis and exhaustive checking, and the checker catches a one-bit corruption. Four, and this is the row that changed: those two lanes are joined now. A searched elite is emitted, re-synthesized by Yosys, and proven by SAT against behavioural addition over the whole input space; corrupting one discovered entry produces a counterexample instead of a pass. A fifth row is sequential repair: one transition behind one flip-flop is rediscovered and proven by induction, with a concrete divergence trace on corruption. One flip-flop is not a processor. Still open are arbitrary topologies, convergence guarantees, coupled or multi-flip-flop repair, and general simplification. There is no area or depth win over ABC, and that is now measured rather than assumed: six circuits, 18 seed results, zero wins, 18 ties, zero losses under one identical mapping recipe.
